Abstract: The big challenge in developing wind energy over the past century, which has focused on environmentally friendly production methods to meet the requirements of modern power systems, is the need for holistic architectures that can cope with variability, connection issues, and sector coupling far beyond conventional electricity-only models. This review offers a critically synthesized, process-level overview of progressive wind–hydrogen hybrids, offering a collective view of advancements in electrical layouts, hydrogen-driven conversion routes, and AI-driven control schemes. In contrast to previous surveys that consider these areas in isolation, we provide an explicit examination of the technical relationships among them, their deployment maturity, and operational trade-offs. The review is a knowledge synthesis of more than 160 peer-reviewed studies published between 2013 and 2026, covering simulation-based research, laboratory model tests, pilot demonstrations, and early utility model installations. Reported data are assessed in the context of experimental and model assumptions. Electrical conversion efficiencies for AC, DC, and hybrid AC/DC architectures typically range from 88%–97% in simulation and laboratory studies. They are lower for field-deployed systems due to protection, filtering, and grid-code compliance requirements—constraint satisfaction. Hence, harmonic distortion below 2%–4% can typically be obtained under controlled conditions by MMC; higher values have been measured in weak grids or unvalidated setups. AI-driven forecasting models, such as the rainbow LSTM hybrids, have achieved sub-10% errors mainly in data-rich simulation/digital twin environments, and real-world accuracy is highly dependent on data quality, spatial resolution, and retraining frequency (216). Documented maintenance cost and degradation-reduction benefits from AI-assisted control are shown to be scenario-specific and often based on simulated or pilot-scale studies with restricted operating conditions. A TRL-based perspective is used to distinguish advanced electrical subsystems (TRL 7–9) from proficient hydrogen conversion technology (TRL 3–8) and AI-enabled real-time control architectures that are predominantly at the demonstration or pilot stage. It discusses additional limitations based on the complexity of system protection, cybersecurity, data integrity, and techno-economic uncertainties, concluding that, in addition to efficiency improvements, scalability is determined by regulatory harmonization, hydrogen certification, and market readiness. In summary, these findings position hybrid wind–hydrogen systems as a promising yet unevenly developed path towards grid-interactive low-carbon energy infrastructures that will require concurrent advances in technology development, policy evolution, and system integration. Title: Construction of Asymmetric Nested Orthogonal Arrays
Source title: Journal of the American Statistical Association
Affiliations: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Henan Normal University, Xinxiang, China; LMAM, School of Mathematical Sciences and Center for Statistical Science, Peking University, Beijing, China; Department of Statistics, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI, United States

Abstract: Nested orthogonal arrays (NOAs), which consist of a pair of orthogonal arrays with one array nested within the other, are extensively used in computer experiments and statistics. They have diverse applications, including data fusion, digital twins, model validation, sequential model evaluation, stochastic programming, chance-constraint problems, nonparametric function estimation, and parameter linking. We propose several general methods for constructing asymmetric NOAs with flexible run sizes, number of levels, and strengths. These methods can generate numerous new classes of NOAs, achieving the maximal number of factors with the minimal run size for both the smaller and larger arrays. A slightly relaxed definition of saturatedness, termed flawless, is introduced for NOAs. Based on the saturated or flawless criteria for the smaller and larger arrays, we classify NOAs into nine types and construct seven new types of NOAs. The newly constructed NOAs with small and moderate run sizes are tabulated for practical use. Title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Industrial Maintenance Optimization
Affiliations: Department Industrial Management, University of Seville, Seville, Spain
Authors with affiliations: Gómez Fernández J.F., Department Industrial Management, University of Seville, Seville, Spain; Crespo Márquez A., Department Industrial Management, University of Seville, Seville, Spain
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) are reshaping maintenance from failure reaction to decision-centric value creation. This chapter synthesizes the state of the art into a practitioner-oriented framework that connects sensing, analytics, and execution across strategic, tactical, and operational levels. We propose a task-driven taxonomy spanning diagnostics, prognostics (RUL with quantified uncertainty), prescriptive optimization, and multi-site orchestration, mapped to data modalities (tabular/events, time-series, images, text, and physics-informed digital twins) and governance constraints (explainability, latency, privacy, maturity). We consolidate enabling architectures—edge/cloud pipelines, data fabric and semantics, MLOps, drift management, XAI, and federated learning—and outline when to prefer classical models, deep learning, probabilistic/survival methods, hybrid physics-informed models, or reinforcement learning. Building on reported industrial impacts, we present a staged roadmap for first deployments with indicative effort, skills, and KPIs, emphasizing how to translate predictions into scheduling, inventory, and risk-based decisions. Finally, we discuss emerging agentic/LLM copilots and Industry 5.0 servitization, highlighting their implications for safety, resilience, and sustainability. The result is a concise guide to select models, design trustworthy pipelines, and scale maintenance optimization with measurable business outcomes. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: A Broadcasting-Based Approach to Create Distributed Situational Awareness in Construction Projects
Source title: IOP Conference Series: Earth and Environmental Science
Affiliations: Department of Design and Manufacturing, Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, India; School of Construction, NICMAR university, Pune, India; Department of Design and Manufacturing, Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, India
Authors with affiliations: Prabhu P., Department of Design and Manufacturing, Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, India; Sahadevan D.V., School of Construction, NICMAR university, Pune, India; Singh V., Department of Design and Manufacturing, Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, India
Abstract: Construction projects operate as temporary socio-technical systems in which interdependent actors must coordinate under uncertainty, making situational awareness (SA) essential for effective decision-making. Although digital technologies such as BIM, IoT, drones, and digital twins improve data visibility, they often centralise information within hierarchical structures, producing uneven awareness across organisational roles. Existing research largely assumes that improved access to information leads to improved awareness, yet limited attention has been given to how communication practices enable distributed actors to develop aligned understanding. This study examines broadcasting as a communication practice through which interpreted project information is simultaneously disseminated to participants to support distributed situational awareness (DSA). Drawing on a qualitative case study of a digitally enabled construction project, the findings show that awareness depends not only on data availability but also on how interpretations are synchronised through communication structures. Broadcast-oriented practices supported shared comprehension and anticipation by reducing delays associated with sequential reporting while complementing existing digital systems. The study contributes to DSA research by demonstrating how communication architecture shapes the emergence of aligned awareness in temporary project environments and highlights broadcasting as a coordination mechanism for improving collective interpretation in digitally enabled construction projects. © 2026, Published under licence by IOP Publishing Ltd. Title: Wireless Environmental Information Theory: A New Paradigm Toward 6G Online and Proactive Environment Intelligence Communication
Affiliations: State Key Laboratory of Networking and Switching Technology, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, 100876, China; Future Research Laboratory, China Mobile Research Institute, Beijing, 100032, China
Authors with affiliations: Zhang J., State Key Laboratory of Networking and Switching Technology, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, 100876, China; Yu L., State Key Laboratory of Networking and Switching Technology, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, 100876, China; Liu S., State Key Laboratory of Networking and Switching Technology, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, 100876, China; Cai Y., State Key Laboratory of Networking and Switching Technology, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, 100876, China; Zhang Y., State Key Laboratory of Networking and Switching Technology, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, 100876, China; Xing H., State Key Laboratory of Networking and Switching Technology, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, 100876, China; Jiang T., Future Research Laboratory, China Mobile Research Institute, Beijing, 100032, China
Abstract: Channels are one of the five critical components of a communication system, and their ergodic capacity is based on all realizations of a statistical channel model. This statistical paradigm has successfully guided the design of mobile communication systems from first generation (1G) to fifth generation (5G). However, this approach relies on offline channel measurements in specific environments, and thus, the system passively adapts to new environments, resulting in deviation from the optimal performance. As sixth generation (6G) expands into ubiquitous environments and pursues higher capacity, numerous sensing and artificial intelligence (AI)-based methods have emerged to combat random channel fading. However, there remains an urgent need for a proactive and online system design paradigm. From a system perspective, we propose an environment intelligence communication (EIC) based on wireless environmental information theory (WEIT) for 6G. The proposed EIC architecture operates in three steps. First, wireless environmental information (WEI) is acquired using sensing techniques. Then, leveraging WEI and channel data, AI techniques are employed to predict channel fading, thereby mitigating channel uncertainty. Finally, the communication system autonomously determines the optimal air–interface transmission strategy based on real-time channel predictions, enabling intelligent interaction with the physical environment. To make this attractive paradigm shift from theory to practice, we establish WEIT for the first time by answering three key problems: How should WEI be defined? Can it be quantified? Does it hold the same properties as statistical communication information? Subsequently, EIC aided by WEI (EIC-WEI) is validated across multiple air–interface tasks, including channel state information prediction, beam prediction, and radio resource management. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed EIC-WEI significantly outperforms the statistical paradigm in decreasing overhead and performance optimization. Finally, several open problems and challenges, including regarding its accuracy, complexity, and generalization, are discussed. This work explores a novel and promising way for integrating communication, sensing, and AI capability in 6G. © 2025 THE AUTHORS

Title: Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Bidding Strategies for Virtual Power Plants in Electricity Spot Markets: A Review
Affiliations: Digital and Intelligent Operations Center, Guangdong Power Grid Co Ltd., Guangdong, Guangzhou, 510600, China
Authors with affiliations: Mo P., Digital and Intelligent Operations Center, Guangdong Power Grid Co Ltd., Guangdong, Guangzhou, 510600, China; Li K., Digital and Intelligent Operations Center, Guangdong Power Grid Co Ltd., Guangdong, Guangzhou, 510600, China; Lu Y., Digital and Intelligent Operations Center, Guangdong Power Grid Co Ltd., Guangdong, Guangzhou, 510600, China; Wen Y., Digital and Intelligent Operations Center, Guangdong Power Grid Co Ltd., Guangdong, Guangzhou, 510600, China; Huang K., Digital and Intelligent Operations Center, Guangdong Power Grid Co Ltd., Guangdong, Guangzhou, 510600, China
Abstract: Electricity spot markets increasingly require flexible, fast, and risk-aware decisions as renewable penetration grows and price volatility intensifies. Virtual power plants (VPPs) aggregate distributed energy resources, storage, and flexible loads to participate in day-ahead and real-time markets, but their bidding decisions must balance profit, operational constraints, and uncertainty. Recent VPP reviews emphasize coordination and market integration challenges, while surveys on reinforcement learning in energy markets highlight the rapid adoption of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. This review focuses on DRL-based bidding strategies for VPPs in electricity spot markets and related competitive settings. Unlike prior reviews that emphasize broad VPP architectures or generic learning applications, we organize the literature around bid formation, market power, risk/safety handling, evaluation comparability, and deployment readiness. We synthesize market structures and bidding rules, VPP modeling assumptions, uncertainty and risk treatments, and DRL algorithm design for single-agent and multi-agent settings. We also compare common simulators, datasets, and evaluation practices, and identify persistent gaps in market-rule fidelity, reward design, adversarial modeling, and live-deployment validation. Finally, we outline future directions including safe and distributionally robust RL, forecasting-coupled bidding, multi-timescale coordination across energy and ancillary services, and digital-twin-based validation.  © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Application review on FMEA/FMECA in marine engineering; [FMEA/FMECA在船舶工程中的应用综述]
Source title: Jiaotong Yunshu Gongcheng Xuebao/Journal of Traffic and Transportation Engineering

Abstract: The basic framework of FMEA/FMECA was summarized in detail. The similarities and differences in the implementation methodologies among three major classification societies were concluded, including China, the United States, and Norway. The specific applications and research hotspots of FMEA/FMECA in the fields of modern ships and marine equipment were further elaborated. The existing difficulties and challenges in the application of FMEA/FMECA were also pointed out. The future development trends of FMEA/FMECA were predicted. Research results indicate that this methodology has been widely applied to the failure and risk assessment of ship power systems, electrical and automation systems, critical hydraulic and piping systems, and various types of marine engineering equipment. Research hotspots focus on how to improve the accuracy and objectivity of FMEA/FMECA, particularly by integrating it with the analytic hierarchy process to scientifically determine the weights of parameters within the risk priority number (RPN), using fuzzy set theory to handle uncertainty and subjectivity in the assessment process, and employing deep learning and big data technologies to dynamically predict real-time failure modes. The difficulties and challenges primarily include insufficient analytical capability for complex integrated systems, a lack of high-quality failure data, and the limitations of traditional RPN calculation methods. FMEA will embrace a more intelligent, systematic, and full life cycle-oriented evolution. The first is data-driven intelligent analysis, which involves using digital twin and artificial intelligence technologies to transition from static assessment to dynamic prediction and predictive health management. The second is the adaptive expansion to address new types of risks, so as to address the novel challenges posed by intelligent autonomous ships and green new-energy vessels. Ultimately, FMEA will be deeply integrated into the full life cycle of ships, from design and operation to maintenance, forming an ever-optimizing closed-loop risk management system. © 2026, Chang'an University. Abstract: Edge General Intelligence (EGI) represents a transformative evolution of edge computing, where distributed agents possess the capability to perceive, reason, and act autonomously across diverse, dynamic environments. This vision is increasingly realized through agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems, which often leverage large language models (LLMs) for complex reasoning and planning. However, language-based reasoning alone struggles to capture high-dimensional physical dynamics. Central to overcoming this challenge are world models, which act as proactive internal simulators that not only predict but also actively imagine future trajectories, reason under uncertainty, and plan multi-step actions with foresight. This proactive nature allows agents to anticipate potential outcomes and optimize decisions ahead of real-world interactions. While prior works in robotics and gaming have showcased the potential of world models, their integration into the wireless edge for EGI remains underexplored. This survey bridges this gap by offering a comprehensive analysis of how world models can empower agentic systems at the edge, enhancing their foresight beyond the limits of LLM-based reasoning. We first examine the architectural foundations of world models, including latent representation learning, dynamics modeling, and imagination-based planning. Building on these core capabilities, we illustrate their proactive applications across EGI scenarios such as vehicular networks, uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) networks, the Internet of Things (IoT) systems, and network functions virtualization, thereby highlighting how they can enhance optimization under latency, energy, and privacy constraints. We then explore their synergy with foundation models and digital twins, positioning world models as the cognitive backbone of EGI. Finally, we highlight open challenges, such as safety guarantees, efficient training, and constrained deployment, and outline future research directions. This survey provides both a conceptual foundation and a practical roadmap for realizing the next generation of intelligent, autonomous edge systems. © 2015 IEEE.

Authors: Yun D.; Kim J.; Lee D.
Title: Development of Early Prediction Model of a CRUD-Induced Power Shift by Applying Autoencoder ML Architecture
Affiliations: Nuclear Engineering Department, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology, Ulsan, South Korea; Analysis, BotBot Inc, Seoul, South Korea
Authors with affiliations: Yun D., Nuclear Engineering Department, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology, Ulsan, South Korea; Kim J., Analysis, BotBot Inc, Seoul, South Korea; Lee D., Nuclear Engineering Department, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology, Ulsan, South Korea
Abstract: This study presents a deep learning framework for the long-horizon forecasting of the axial shape index (ASI) to support a few-months early detection of the CRUD-induced power shift (CIPS) in pressurized water reactors. CRUD accumulation and boron hideout, which drive the axial offset anomaly (AOA), are difficult to observe directly in operating plants, motivating the use of data-driven inference models trained on synthetic multiphysics simulations. Using STREAM/RAST-K with CRUD deposition and power-transient modeling, an extensive spatial-temporal data set was generated to represent both full-power and seasonal power decrement operations. Three architectures, a long-short-term memory (LSTM)-based autoencoder (LBAE), a transformer-based autoencoder (TBAE), and a hybrid convolutional neural network–LSTM-transformer (CLT), were trained using staged learning, scheduled sampling, and autoregressive rollout to improve long-sequence stability. The CLT model achieved a mean absolute error of 0.000264 for a 300-day ASI prediction under full-power conditions and 0.000320 under 10-day power decrement scenarios, indicating moderate sensitivity to transient operations. Comparative evaluations showed that the TBAE and CLT models generalized effectively to long-range predictions, maintaining errors within approximately 1% of the allowable ASI margin. These results suggest that hybrid spatial-temporal deep learning models can function as digital twin components for monitoring CRUD evolution and providing a proactive CIPS risk assessment during reactor operation, pointing toward future extensions with multiphysics coupling and uncertainty quantification. © 2026 American Nuclear Society.

Title: Comprehensive Evaluation of Hybrid Utilization of DT and Virtual Power Plant Platforms for Distributed Energy Resource Management
Affiliations: Energy Systems Engineering, Ankara Yildirim Beyazıt University, Ankara, 06090, Turkey
Authors with affiliations: Onsomu O.N., Energy Systems Engineering, Ankara Yildirim Beyazıt University, Ankara, 06090, Turkey; Şen O., Energy Systems Engineering, Ankara Yildirim Beyazıt University, Ankara, 06090, Turkey; Yeşilata B., Energy Systems Engineering, Ankara Yildirim Beyazıt University, Ankara, 06090, Turkey
Abstract: As the global energy sector seeks to reduce dependence on fossil fuel–based generation and mitigate carbon emissions, there is an increasing need to evaluate advanced enabling platforms that support sustainable energy integration. Technologies, such as digital twin (DT) and virtual power plant (VPP), provide enhanced capabilities for detailed modeling, monitoring, and optimization of modern power systems with high penetration of renewable energy sources (RESs). This study proposes an integrated DT–VPP framework for effective management of distributed energy resources (DERs), particularly photovoltaic (PV) systems, while also presenting a wind turbine (WT) simulation case using distributionally robust optimization (DRO) to improve grid stability under uncertainty. The proposed framework enables real-time asset monitoring, operational optimization, and enhanced decision-making to mitigate technical constraints such as power losses, capacity limitations, and renewable intermittency. Furthermore, the study highlights the role of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven strategies in improving predictive analytics, system reliability, and resilience of future smart grids. The findings demonstrate that the integration of DT, VPP, and AI-based optimization techniques can significantly enhance grid stability, operational flexibility, and sustainable energy management. Title: Life cycle assessment of mixed-use buildings with varying HVAC systems in different climates for sustainable-responsive design and low-carbon solutions
Affiliations: School of Energy Engineering and Sustainable Resources, University of Tehran, Tehran, Iran
Authors with affiliations: Mobaraki M.M., School of Energy Engineering and Sustainable Resources, University of Tehran, Tehran, Iran; Zahedi R., School of Energy Engineering and Sustainable Resources, University of Tehran, Tehran, Iran; Yousefi H., School of Energy Engineering and Sustainable Resources, University of Tehran, Tehran, Iran; Noorollahi Y., School of Energy Engineering and Sustainable Resources, University of Tehran, Tehran, Iran
Abstract: This study conducts a comprehensive Whole Building Life Cycle Assessment (WBLCA) of a 3,450 m² commercial-residential mixed-use building located across four climatically distinct cities in Iran: Tehran (semi-arid), Rasht (humid), Yazd (hot-dry), and Mashhad (cold-dry). Three commonly used HVAC configurations—(i) air-cooled chiller with natural gas furnace, (ii) 2-pipe fan coil units, and (iii) DX split heat pumps—are evaluated across twelve climate-system scenarios. A Building Information Modeling (BIM) platform integrated with Carrier HAP 4.9 and SimaPro 9.0 (ReCiPe 2016 H, Ecoinvent v3) was employed to simulate building energy loads and quantify cradle-to-grave environmental impacts. Results indicate that DX split systems reduce total life-cycle carbon emissions by up to 40% compared to centralized systems, particularly in hot and humid zones. Embodied carbon analysis revealed concrete as the most dominant contributor, accounting for 68% of upstream emissions. Substitution with low-carbon Leca-based concrete selected from the Ecoinvent library led to a 12% reduction in embodied impacts. Sensitivity analysis showed that a one-unit increase in HVAC COP can cut operational emissions by approximately 28%. Uncertainty was evaluated using a Monte-Carlo simulation (n = 1,000), confirming robustness within a ±9% margin. A blind-run validation approach, calibrated using hourly simulation data and benchmarking against the technical dossier of a comparable case, demonstrated acceptable predictive accuracy (MBE = 4.2%, CVRMSE = 1.03%). The study's novelty lies in its climate-responsive scenario matrix, integration of real equipment data, and its end-to-end automated workflow from BIM modeling to impact assessment. The findings highlight the importance of climate-adaptive HVAC design, use of localized low-impact materials, and digital modelling integration to support national decarbonization goals. Recommendations for future work include incorporating economic and social dimensions into LCA, exploring hybrid HVAC technologies, and applying digital twins for real-time performance feedback. © 2025 Elsevier Ltd

Title: INVERSE ESTIMATION OF DIRECTIONAL WAVE SPECTRUM AND STRESS RESPONSE RECONSTRUCTION AT UNMEASURED LOCATIONS OF A 9,000 TEU CLASS CONTAINER SHIP USING FULL-SCALE MEASUREMENT DATA
Source title: Proceedings of the International Conference on Offshore Mechanics and Arctic Engineering - OMAE
Affiliations: INHA University, Incheon, South Korea; HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, Gyeonggi, South Korea
Authors with affiliations: Son J., INHA University, Incheon, South Korea; Kim Y., INHA University, Incheon, South Korea; Lee J., HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, Gyeonggi, South Korea; Jung B., HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, Gyeonggi, South Korea
Abstract: Ensuring the structural integrity of a vessel during operation is a critical yet challenging task, as the structural response to ocean waves involves significant uncertainties arising from complex environmental and operational conditions. The digital twin technology, which integrates real measurement data with a vessel’s digital design model, has been increasingly recognized as an effective means of ensuring structural integrity under operational conditions. Within this framework, accurate estimation of the directional wave spectrum plays a key role, as it enables the characterization of sea states and supports the estimation of structural responses at unmeasured locations. This study employs a regularized optimization formulation combined with a cubic B-spline surface representation to estimate the directional wave spectrum from onboard measurement data. The proposed approach minimizes the discrepancy between the measured and reconstructed response spectra while maintaining the smoothness and continuity of the estimated surface. An adaptive quadrature scheme is also introduced to address the singularity that arises in the encounter-to-absolute frequency conversion due to the Doppler effect. The methodology is applied to long-term onboard measurement data obtained from a 9,000 TEU CLASS container vessel. The estimated directional wave spectra were statistically analyzed to evaluate their consistency across varying sea states, and the reconstructed response spectra were compared with the measured counterparts to validate the accuracy of the estimation procedure. These results demonstrate the applicability of the proposed approach to structural integrity assessment under operating conditions. Copyright © 2026 by ASME.

Title: Mapping Emerging Trends in Artificial Intelligence for Quality Control and Management: A Large-Scale Computational Literature Review Using Semantic Natural Language Processing
Affiliations: Laboratory of Research and Development in Engineering Sciences, Faculty of Sciences and Techniques Al-Hoceima, Abdelmalek Essaadi University, Tetouan, Morocco
Authors with affiliations: Afassi O., Laboratory of Research and Development in Engineering Sciences, Faculty of Sciences and Techniques Al-Hoceima, Abdelmalek Essaadi University, Tetouan, Morocco; Benaya N., Laboratory of Research and Development in Engineering Sciences, Faculty of Sciences and Techniques Al-Hoceima, Abdelmalek Essaadi University, Tetouan, Morocco; Dib F., Laboratory of Research and Development in Engineering Sciences, Faculty of Sciences and Techniques Al-Hoceima, Abdelmalek Essaadi University, Tetouan, Morocco
Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into industrial quality control (QC) and management encompassing automated defect detection, real-time process monitoring, and zero-defect manufacturing has generated a rapidly expanding yet fragmented research landscape. This study addresses the need for comprehensive mapping of quality and reliability engineering practice through a computational systematic review of 9618 publications spanning the 2020–2025 period. A hybrid natural language processing (NLP) pipeline combining FlashText, Sentence-BERT, KeyBERT, and spaCy performs semantic extraction of AI architectures, learning paradigms, defect typologies, and deployment contexts. The review pursues three objectives: mapping the architectural evolution of deep learning in industrial inspection, characterizing operational challenges of AI-driven manufacturing, and identifying methodological frontiers for improving production reliability and supporting intelligent quality assurance (QA) systems. Results reveal that AI-based quality control advances through coevolution of neural architectures, learning paradigms, and deployment requirements. CNNs remain central to discriminative visual inspection, while Transformers extend capabilities for multimodal reasoning. The field exhibits strong bias toward surface defects while overlooking safety-critical internal defects. Emerging trends show transition from algorithm-centric research toward deployment-oriented paradigms including Uncertainty Quantification, Edge AI, Explainable AI, and Digital Twins. This work provides practitioners with an evidence-based foundation for developing reliable, scalable AI quality systems aligned with Industry 4.0 principles. © 2026 John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

Abstract: Automotive production planning has become increasingly complicated and its structures and processes difficult to manage as a result of planning volatility, disruptions to logistical flow and urgent customer demand for increasing availability of customization. Digital solutions that have developed from Industry 4.0 technologies such as artificial intelligence have and continue to create opportunities to automate decision making, resource management, and demand forecasting. However industrial systems and complex continuity of operations have taken critical damage from recent crises (primarily COVID-19) and these events have highlighted the fragility of planning within the context of the disruption cycles of Industry 4.0 planning. In this context, resilience has emerged as a critical capability, defined as the ability of systems to absorb shocks, adapt to change, and maintain operational continuity. In this study, the complexity of the notion resilience will be compared with two models of industrial planning: one rooted in the Industry 4.0 sector predictive performance models; the second is built in the future notion of Industry 5.0, which builds on elements of resilience, flexibility and human-machine alliances. The analysis reflects a lit review demonstrating recent findings, and illustrated with examples in the European automotive sector, the analysis uses a multidimensional evaluation grid of the two models of planning, covering criteria such as agility, robustness, transparency and human integration. Quantitative results show that Industry 4.0 outperforms in accuracy (57.1%) while Industry 5.0 leads in flexibility (57.1%), robustness (58.3%), agility (56.2%), transparency (63.6%), and human-machine integration (72.7%). The findings demonstrate both paradigms, while showing some differences, are complementary, and postulate the idea of a hybrid planning system. The importance of digital twins, explainable AI and other collaborative interface technologies as a means of adapting and maintaining continuity when planning in conditions of uncertainty will be examined. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Abstract: This work examined the combined effects of waste cooking oil biodiesel (WCOB), NiFe2O4 nanocatalysts, and hydrogen (H2) enrichment on in-cylinder processes, engine performance, and emissions of a diesel engine. To accurately represent the physical processes and to derive thermodynamically consistent predictions, a physics-encoded multi-task machine learning (PE-MTMML) model was developed. Tests were carried out on a single-cylinder, four-stroke diesel engine at 1500 rpm. The engine was operated on blends of diesel, WCOB, and NiFe2O4 (50–150 ppm) with the addition of H2 at 5 LPM. The analysis of combustion was done based on the measurement of in-cylinder pressure with respect to the crank angle from which peak pressure and heat release rate (HRR) were derived using a single-zone model. Performance parameters were obtained at various loads through the full load range. The PE-MTMML model incorporated not only the thermodynamic reciprocity but also catalytic oxidation trends and root-sum-square (RSS) uncertainty constraints. At full load, the NiFe2O4 nanoparticles improved catalytic oxidation and premixed combustion, thus, the peak pressure rose by 7.8% at most, and HRR by 14% compared to diesel. The ensemble of WCOB + NiFe2O4 150 ppm + H2 led to an increase in brake thermal efficiency (BTE) of 29.2% and a decrease in brake-specific energy consumption (BSEC) of 22.3% in comparison with diesel. Inspection of emissions revealed that the smoke opacity was lessened by 10.9%, carbon monoxide (CO) by 20%, and hydrocarbons (HC) by 25%, while nitrogen oxides (NOx) were elevated by 7.5% relative to diesel. The PE-MTMML model had excellent prediction capabilities (mean R2 = 0.9993) and at the same time adhered to thermodynamic constraints. The synergistic effect of NiFe2O4 nanocatalysis and H2 enrichment makes WCOB both a high-efficiency and a low-pollution fuel. By allowing for optimization with minimal experimental input, the PE-MTMML scheme acts as a trustworthy digital twin, supporting circular-economy goals and the transition to sustainable, carbon-neutral diesel engines. Title: CLAIR: SLA-Aware Inference Routing in Converged Cloud-Network Systems

Abstract: Deploying mission-critical AI services across converged cloud-network systems necessitates a delicate balance between diagnostic accuracy and service latency, a challenge exacerbated by stochastic network fluctuations. Existing offloading strategies typically rely on infrastructure-level metrics, often overlooking the intrinsic uncertainty of inference tasks and failing to strictly adhere to Service Level Agreements (SLAs). To bridge this gap, we propose CLAIR, a ConfidenceLatency Adaptive Inference Routing framework. CLAIR employs a confidence-gated mechanism that processes high-confidence, routine tasks at the edge while offloading ambiguous, lowconfidence samples to the cloud for expert reasoning. Crucially, to ensure SLA compliance under dynamic network conditions, we introduce Latency-Constrained Adaptive Thresholding (LCAT). This feedback-driven controller utilizes an AIMD-like strategy to dynamically modulate the offloading confidence threshold based on real-time latency observations. Experiments on a digital twin fault diagnosis testbed show that, in the evaluated setting, CLAIR achieves a more favorable accuracy-latency trade-off than stateof-the-art baselines. Quantitatively, the framework attains a steady-state accuracy of 88%-providing a 13% gain over pureedge execution-while reducing average end-to-end latency by 26% compared to queue-based heuristics, effectively preventing SLA violations during network congestion. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: The representation of geographic processes is essential for revealing their evolutionary patterns and mechanisms over space and time. However, existing spatiotemporal data models mainly focus on historical change and are limited in representing future evolution and the interrelationships among heterogeneous geographic processes, which constrains prospective spatiotemporal analysis. This study presents a novel spatiotemporal data model to describe the historical and future evolution and associations of geographic processes within a geographic system. Unlike historical evolution, which is typically deterministic, the proposed model represents future evolution as inherently uncertain, defined along two dimensions: (1) conditional uncertainty—future states may take multiple possible forms under different driving conditions; and (2) temporal uncertainty—future states evolve continuously as new historical states emerge. An update approach based on deep neural network-based spatiotemporal prediction models is introduced to dynamically generate future states of geographic processes. Finally, the experiment on three interrelated geographic processes in an island system shows that the proposed model can provide a new perspective integrating history and future to analyse the spatiotemporal evolution of both single processes and multiple processes. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: CausalTwinOps: Governance-Gated Counterfactual Repair Verification for Enterprise Data Pipelines
Affiliations: Federal Express Corporation, Dallas, TX, United States
Authors with affiliations: Konduru R.K., Federal Express Corporation, Dallas, TX, United States
Abstract: Enterprise data-pipeline incidents can propagate across latency, freshness, completeness, validity, cost, and governance metrics, so recovery requires more than anomaly detection or root-cause ranking. This paper presents CausalTwinOps, a governance-gated counterfactual repair-verification framework that separates root-cause nomination from repair acceptance. The evaluated implementation uses a fixed, domain-defined fault vocabulary, an auditable ordinary-least-squares response model with selected interaction terms, counterfactual feature interventions, a template repair library, and explicit service and governance constraints. The present study focuses on offline, window-level repair verification with interpretable intervention semantics; online causal discovery, learned repair policies, and continuous twin synchronization are natural extensions beyond the evaluated scope. Across four random seeds and 489 synthetic incident cases, CausalTwinOps obtains 95.3% mean root-cause accuracy and 99.0% top-2 accuracy. Several supervised classifiers trained directly on the synthetic root labels obtain higher classification accuracy, which highlights the complementary roles of fault nomination and repair verification. The distinguishing result is the verification stage: removing the governance gate raises mean repair acceptance from 63.5% to 99.2% but yields 162 unsafe accepted repairs, whereas the configured full verifier yields none under the benchmark’s policy-risk and validity constraints within the simulator. This zero count is a compliance result relative to the configured simulator rules, not evidence that unmodeled real-world harms are impossible. The core contribution is thus a decision layer that tests whether a candidate repair is predicted to improve downstream state while remaining inside configured safety constraints. The controlled simulator provides a reproducible setting for characterizing mechanism behavior under known assumptions. To support the next validation stage, we report seed-level uncertainty, make causal and statistical assumptions explicit, and define a concrete external-validation protocol for real or semi-real incident data. © 2013 IEEE.

Title: Machine-Learning-Driven Production Optimization in Automotive Closed-Loop Supply Chains under Remanufacturing Cost Disruptions
Affiliations: School of Digital Economy and Management, Software Engineering Institute of Guangzhou, Guangzhou, China; Department of Economics and Management, Zhanjiang Preschool Education College, Zhanjiang, China; School of Business, Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, Guangzhou, China
Authors with affiliations: Wu H., School of Digital Economy and Management, Software Engineering Institute of Guangzhou, Guangzhou, China; Yang Q., Department of Economics and Management, Zhanjiang Preschool Education College, Zhanjiang, China; Zhang L., School of Business, Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, Guangzhou, China
Abstract: Leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to optimize closed-loop supply chain management, this study advances the frontier of digital sustainable manufacturing within the automotive industry by addressing dynamic production decision-making under remanufacturing cost disruptions. While automotive closed-loop supply chains offer significant economic and environmental benefits through automotive recycling and remanufacturing processes, their operational resilience is increasingly challenged by emergent disruptions and escalating uncertainties. To bridge this gap, we develop a robust analytical framework that integrates remanufacturing cost disruption parameters into production optimization models for automotive remanufacturing systems. The findings suggest that the optimal retail price and production quantity both have some robustness, while the optimal collection rate always changes under remanufacturing cost disruption. It is also observed that the centralized decisionmaker and automobile manufacturer prefer to revise decisions when facing disruption; the automobile retailer also wants to adjust decisions when facing considerably negative disruption, but tends to maintain original decisions when facing considerably positive disruption. The proposed models enable proactive disruption management through scenario-based optimization, facilitating digital twin implementations in smart manufacturing systems. Ultimately, numerical experiments using industry-specific parameters validate the model's predictive accuracy and demonstrate its practical applicability in real-world automotive closed-loop supply chains. The proposed machine-learning-driven decision-making model can be further exploited for optimizing risk mitigation strategy design in automotive closed-loop supply chains, particularly by enabling adaptive responses to remanufacturing cost disruptions through dynamic production reconfiguration and cost-sensitive resource allocation. © The Institution of Engineering and Technology 2025.

Abstract: The widespread adoption of smart buildings and digital twin technologies enables the continuous and real-time collection of extensive data on key parameters and performance of buildings. The analysis of these data through techniques of probabilistic machine learning provides confident predictive models of the building performances, which in turn allow enhanced methodologies of sustainable and resilient building design. Building seismic performance is crucial for earthquake resilience. Beyond the primary objectives of ensuring safety and preventing collapse, the seismic performance of a building can be assessed by examining its ability to maintain functionality and minimize repair costs. Recent studies have demonstrated that resilient buildings exert a lower environmental impact over their lifecycle, due to reduced repair/maintenance stages. It follows that resilience is a key requisite for sustainable design. In this paper, an integrated design procedure is introduced for optimizing structural seismic safety and energy efficiency of buildings under imprecise and limited information. More specifically, seismic excitation is modeled as a zero-mean stationary Gaussian random process; to take into account epistemic uncertainties, the parameters of the underlying Power Spectral Density function are described as interval variables. Data on energy consumption are measured through a network of sensors. Given the available information, energy forecasting is accomplished through Recurrent Neural Networks. The propagation of uncertainties is accomplished through the framework of Sustainable and Resilient Engineering using HAZUS, a methodology developed by FEMA to estimate potential losses from natural disasters. The two performances, i.e., seismic and energy costs, are then combined with Multi-Attribute Utility theory. A building example shows the attractive features of the proposed procedure. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: Digital Transformation of the Energy Ecosystem: Opportunities, Challenges, and Pathways to Sustainability
Affiliations: Istanbul Okan University, Istanbul, Turkey
Authors with affiliations: Alp S., Istanbul Okan University, Istanbul, Turkey
Abstract: This chapter examines how the energy sector is progressing through digitalization, highlighting its opportunities, challenges, and impact on sustainability. Technologies like AI, big data, blockchain, smart grids, and digital twins are changing the way energy is produced, distributed, and consumed. They provide real-time data and tools that enable more innovative resource management, enhance operational efficiency, increase prosumer participation, and support low-carbon transitions. However, digitalization also introduces challenges, such as cybersecurity threats, regulatory uncertainties, infrastructure problems, and environmental issues related to data centers and blockchain systems. It emphasizes the importance of fair and equal digital access, digital literacy, and governance to ensure a just energy transition. The chapter advocates for digital policies aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and strategies at various levels that address ethical, environmental, and socio-economic concerns. While digitalization offers many benefits, it also presents risks that can be mitigated through more thoughtful and inclusive policies. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: Non-stationary active learning for structural state inverse prediction

Abstract: Accurately inferring in-service loads and internal states is essential for life prediction, anomaly detection, and digital-twin updating of critical structures. Structural load and state inversion is hindered by non-stationary responses, multiple admissible solutions, and costly forward evaluations. We propose a sample-efficient inverse prediction method that combines Rotating Importance Acquisition (RIA) with Adaptive Interval Refinement (AIR). RIA enriches a Gaussian process (GP) surrogate by rotating a small leave-out subset to obtain out-of-subset likelihood exposure scores. These scores are fused with normalized predictive uncertainty so sampling concentrates on regions that are both misfit and uncertain, allocating more evaluations to locally non-stationary zones. AIR operates on the updated GP to achieve multi-solution inverse prediction: feasible parameter intervals are progressively refined, candidates are clustered into distinct solution basins to balance diversity, and representative solutions with dispersion measures are extracted until stability criteria are met. Benchmarks on nonlinear test functions show higher surrogate accuracy and better sample efficiency than standard GP, K-Fold ANN, and Interquartile Range (IQR) baselines. The inversion stage recovers multiple well-separated solution basins with low identification error. A turbine disk load reconstruction case using high-fidelity finite element analysis confirms robustness and practical applicability. The method provides a unified, data-efficient framework for non-stationary multi-solution structural load inversion and state monitoring. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2025.

Author full names: Amiri, Mohsen (58924796700); Avrachenkov, Konstantin (35583036400); El Mimouni, Ibtihal (59659326700); Magnusson, Sindri (56810738200)
Title: MARBLE: Multi-Armed Restless Bandits in Latent Markovian Environment
Source title: European Control Conference (Piscataway, N.J. Online), ECC
Abstract: Restless Multi-Armed Bandits (RMABs) are powerful models for decision-making under uncertainty, yet classical formulations typically assume fixed dynamics, an assumption often violated in nonstationary environments. We introduce MARBLE (Multi-Armed Restless Bandits in a Latent Markovian Environment), which augments RMABs with a latent Markov state that induces nonstationary behavior. In MARBLE, each arm evolves according to a latent environment state that switches over time, making policy learning substantially more challenging. We further introduce the Markov-Averaged Indexability (MAI) criterion as a relaxed indexability assumption and prove that, despite unobserved regime switches, under the MAI criterion, synchronous Q-learning with Whittle Indices (QWI) converges almost surely to the optimal Q-function and the corresponding Whittle indices. We validate MARBLE on a calibrated simulator-embedded (digital twin) recommender system, where QWI consistently adapts to a shifting latent state and converges to an optimal policy, empirically corroborating our theoretical findings. © 2026 EUCA.

Abstract: Continuous cardiovascular monitoring creates a distributed scientific workflow in which Internet of Things (IoT) devices acquire physiological streams while patient-level records remain local. This paper presents PhysioFed-Discover, a physiological-constraint federated learning (FL) framework for cardiovascular representation modeling and cross-client knowledge discovery. Sensor-aware tokens and latent cardiovascular proxies support task prediction together with soft constraints for heart-rate consistency, ECG–PPG timing, Windkessel pressure dynamics, monotonic blood-pressure relations, and plausible ranges. The server combines sample support, predictive uncertainty, update drift, and physiological residuals to weight compressed updates; label-conditioned prototypes summarize recurring representation patterns. Experiments on real patient recordings cover ECG diagnosis on PTB-XL, blood-pressure estimation on PulseDB, and hypotension forecasting on VitalDB. Relative to Transformer-FL, the PTB-XL macro-area under the receiver operating characteristic curve increases from 0.899 to 0.914, PulseDB systolic-pressure mean absolute error decreases from 8.18 to 7.48 mmHg, and VitalDB area under the curve increases from 0.862 to 0.881. Module-level ablations support further study of the combined framework but do not isolate each physiological mechanism. The evaluation retrospectively analyzes patient recordings from the three public datasets, with these records partitioned among federated clients. Knowledge discovery denotes exploratory inspection of task-conditioned prototypes, not validated clinical phenotypes or a patient-specific mechanistic digital twin. © 2014 IEEE.

Author full names: Iaselli, Nicolò (59761784700); Lorenzi, Stefano (55480869500)
Title: Monte Carlo–Informed Surrogate Model for the Analysis of Decay Heat Behavior in Molten Salt Reactors
Affiliations: Department of Energy, CeSNEF - Nuclear Engineering Division, Politecnico di Milano, Milan, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Iaselli N., Department of Energy, CeSNEF - Nuclear Engineering Division, Politecnico di Milano, Milan, Italy; Lorenzi S., Department of Energy, CeSNEF - Nuclear Engineering Division, Politecnico di Milano, Milan, Italy
Abstract: Noble metal fission products in molten salt reactors (MSRs) deposit on primary loop surfaces, where their decay heat becomes safety-relevant during drain scenarios: Once the salt is discharged, the deposit remains without active cooling and can drive localized overheating. Predicting it requires tracking the full nuclide inventory across core, bulk, and deposition regions, for which repeated Monte Carlo (MC) depletion is prohibitive. This work develops a MC-informed surrogate built on a sparse transition operator spanning neutron-induced reactions, decay, advection, and deposition, with region-wise mass transfer correlations setting the deposition rates. The neutron-induced rates are extracted from a single MC simulation and rescaled with power under a constant-spectrum assumption, so that the ordinary differential equations (ODEs) system is solved without further transport runs, for a substantially larger nuclide set than historical zero-dimensional models. Applied to the Molten Salt Reactor Experiment (MSRE) fuel loop, the predicted mass transfer coefficients reproduce the original MSRE values, and the calculated 132Te distribution is comparable across surfaces for both the 233U and 235U campaigns without per-nuclide tuning. Benchmarked against a self-consistent MC workflow on a simplified generic MSR case, the surrogate reproduces the total decay heat of both the bulk and deposition nodes from sub-second to yearly time scales, to within ±0.3% at fixed power and ~2% under sinusoidal modulation. It does so at a cost low enough for design exploration and for a digital-twin representation of the primary loop. An uncertainty quantification shows that fission yields dominate the nuclear data budget and that the deposited inventory is markedly more uncertain than the bulk, partly due to non–noble-metal precursors in the yield normalization constraint. © 2026 American Nuclear Society.

Title: Road use as conversation: a Multimodal Multi-scale Coordinated Action Model (MCAM) for immersive and generative traffic safety applications
Affiliations: Department of Geoinformatics (Z_GIS), University of Salzburg, Salzburg, Austria; Department of Applied Linguistics, University of Salzburg, Salzburg, Austria; Geo-social AI lab, IT:U Interdisciplinary Transformation University, Linz, Austria

Abstract: Understanding how VRUs—pedestrians, cyclists, and micromobility users—coordinate social action and resolve conflict in mixed-mode urban traffic is not merely a technological but a fundamental human factors problem. The challenge concerns how people perceive, attend to, and act upon the behavioral signals of others under real-world conditions of unpredictability and uncertainty. Intention prediction is a key mechanism through which traffic safety applications attempt to manage this complexity, yet existing frameworks treat coordination as a binary classification task and fail to capture its multi-scale, gradient nature. Current research has major gaps related to data, robustness, and contextual understanding. XR and digital twin systems are deployed for urban traffic safety, yet a critical validity problem persists: these systems are designed and evaluated without ground-truth knowledge of how people look, move, and experience cognitive load in real mixed-mode traffic. Simulator-based studies offer control but sacrifice ecological validity; existing real-world datasets are vehicle-centric, single-modality, and restricted to pedestrian-crossing scenarios. This paper introduces the MCAM, a theoretical framework that reconceptualises urban mobility as structured communicative interaction governed by shared behavioral conventions across three spatiotemporal scales—micro (1–5 s), meso (5–30 s), and macro (longer-term contextual)—operationalising conflict as a five-phase gradient progression from coordinated flow to conflict event. MCAM is operationalised through a multimodal field study using a BIBD at three ecologically distinct urban sites (a signalized intersection, a shared space, and a cycling corridor), observed across peak hours and seasonal conditions. Thirty gender- and age-balanced participants each navigate all three sites as pedestrians, cyclists, and e-scooter riders—a within-subject cross-modal design is often absent from the majority of existing intention detection datasets— would give approximately 60 h of usable recording and 1, 500 hours of annotation. Three contributions are presented: (1) a reusable multimodal field methodology for ecologically valid human factors data collection; (2) an MCAM-grounded annotation scheme applicable to both real and simulated environments; and (3) a methodological bridge between real-world human behavior and the design of immersive and generative traffic safety applications. Title: The Agentic Control Framework: Integrating Knowledge Graph Retrieval and Game-Theoretic Multi-Agent Learning for Robust Process Design

Affiliations: DTx - Digital Transformation CoLab, Guimarães, 4800-058, Portugal; University of Minho, School of Engineering, Guimarães, Portugal

Abstract: The realization of resilient autonomous systems is currently impeded by the difficulty of translating abstract design requirements into verifiable control policies that can withstand significant model uncertainty. Here we present the Agentic Control Framework, a full-stack neuro-symbolic architecture that unifies semantic reasoning with game-theoretic hardening to maximize robustness. The workflow initiates with a Large Language Model (LLM)-based agent that leverages a domainspecific Knowledge Graph to comprehend unstructured design specifications and retrieve optimal control constraints. These formal specifications characterize a high-fidelity Digital Twin, which incorporates a Reduced Order Model (ROM) integrated via Runge-Kutta (RK4) methods. Within this adaptive environment, we solve the robust control problem as a multi-agent zero-sum differential game using Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), where a stabilizing Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) policy competes against an adversary injecting worst-case stochastic disturbances. We benchmark this adversarial formulation against classical H∞ synthesis and standard Vanilla PPO, demonstrating that the system converges to an empirical Nash Equilibrium that rivals theoretical robust control baselines. Our results indicate that grounding agentic comprehension in rigorous game-theoretic training produces self-organizing controllers that maintain operational stability under severe uncertainty, bridging the gap between theoretical robust control and adaptive autonomy. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: The rapid and future perspectives on sustainable smart cities’ ever-increasing growth of the global urban population of the 21st century raises the question of how we can transform cities into spaces that not only support the efficiency of urban processes but also resolve urgent sustainability issues. Drawing on a cognitive technology discussion in this chapter, the author explores the possibilities of change in regard to the future of sustainable smart cities. This is because urban management can be enhanced through the incorporation of applications for artificial intelligence (AI), block chain, and digital twin models in decision making and monitoring of urban processes and systems in real time and resource optimization, including offering protection against natural uncertainties such as climate change and natural disasters. The major emerging trend is fundamentally redefining sustainability in the urban context. Self-organized systems of the city, enabled by block chains and distributed ledgers and formally nonhierarchical, provide new possibilities for democratic organization and participation. The exchange of microgrids between neighbors shows that sustainable energy is a way forward economically and environmentally. AI-based circular economy models help improve recycling and reduce waste and, in the process, reduce environmental impacts. The use of computer-generated virtual copies of urban environments as modelling tools helps to predict the problems a city may face and prepare their solution. Moreover, 5G and the advancements of the subsequent generations of connectivity provide the necessary basis for the massive scale of the IoT to provide the fundamental structure for smooth, real-time urban functioning. The set of these technologies enables better management of the demands of modern living by cities, ranging from traffic control to climate change adaptation. Sociocognitive innovations other than technology are constructing options for democratic and engaging urban citizenship experiences. AI-assisted consumer-centric public services driven by data analytics provide relevant services to provide satisfaction and convenience. Rubber stamp intensification of disaster prediction and response clarify the development and solidification of urban intensification, making it possible for cities to be ‘disaster proof’ and be able to recover from a disaster soonest. On the other hand, smart platforms play the role of hubs that bring together stakeholders to share information and make joint decisions in the interest of sustainable development. © 2026 by Nova Science Publishers, Inc.

Abstract: The deep integration of high-resolution Earth observation, artificial intelligence, and the Internet of Things is propelling remote sensing geological exploration from traditional single-satellite data interpretation towards a new paradigm of space-air-ground collaborative observation and intelligent multi-source data analysis. This paper systematically reviews the key progress of the integrated "space-based (satellites), air-based (aviation/ UAVs), and ground-based (surface sensing)" remote sensing technology system in the field of mineral exploration. The discussion focuses on three primary aspects: (1) Breakthroughs in platform and sensor technologies, particularly the advancements in hyperspectral, LiDAR, and synthetic aperture radar, along with their collaborative observation mechanisms and current applications; (2) Innovations in intelligent data processing methods, encompassing fusion techniques for multi-source heterogeneous data, as well as AI-driven extraction of mineral information and metallogenic prediction models; (3) Establishment and practice of application paradigms, summarizing successful case studies of this technology in complex scenarios such as covered areas, deep-seated zones, and special landscape regions. This has led to the development of a standardized technical workflow: "satellite-based wide-area screening→UAV-based detailed survey→ground-based target validation." Building on this systematic review, the paper further analyzes the core technological bottlenecks currently hindering development. These primarily include the lack of standardization in multi-source data fusion, difficulties in quantifying prediction uncertainty, and the weak interpretability of intelligent geological models (the "black box" problem). Looking forward, the paper discusses future development trends, highlighting that real-time, intelligent, and digital-twin-enabled smart exploration, along with the construction of satellite constellation-coordinated intelligent observation networks, will become important drivers of innovation in remote sensing technology for mineral exploration. In conclusion, this intelligent space-air-ground integrated remote sensing technology system is fundamentally transforming traditional exploration paradigms, providing critical scientific and technological support for solving exploration challenges in complex geological settings and ensuring national mineral resource security. © (2026), (Editorial Board of Geology and Exploration). Abstract: Modern Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) must be autonomously adaptable to deal with growing complexity and uncertainty in the environment. In this paper, the author proposes a scalable agentic AI architecture that will allow CPS to sense, think, and act in autonomy. The framework combined both local edge intelligence and global coordination to solve this by balancing the distributed agents with the hierarchical reinforcement learning. By contrast with the traditional centralized models, our architecture employs the use of selfmonitoring and feedback loops in the optimization of performance in real time and without human intervention. Assessment of various CPS conditions reveals major gains in decision quality, latency, and resiliency, providing a solid base to the future of the industrial automation and intelligent infrastructure.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Reviews of the Static, Adoptive, and Dynamic Sampling in Wafer Manufacturing
Affiliations: Africa Industrial Research Center, National Chung Hsing University, Taichung, 40227, Taiwan; Department of Bio-Industrial Mechatronics Engineering, National Chung Hsing University, Taichung, 40227, Taiwan
Authors with affiliations: Chen H.-Y., Africa Industrial Research Center, National Chung Hsing University, Taichung, 40227, Taiwan; Chen C., Department of Bio-Industrial Mechatronics Engineering, National Chung Hsing University, Taichung, 40227, Taiwan
Abstract: Semiconductor wafer manufacturing is one of the most complex and data-intensive processes in the industry, encompassing the front-end (FEOL), middle-end (MOL), and back-end (BEOL) stages, involving thousands of interdependent processes. Each stage can introduce potential variability, thereby reducing yield, making metrology and inspection crucial for process control. However, due to capacity, cost, and destructive testing constraints, exhaustive metrology for every wafer or die is impractical. Therefore, this study aims to introduce sampling strategies that have evolved to balance the accuracy, risk, and efficiency of measurement allocation. This review presents a literature review of static, adaptive, and dynamic sampling and discusses recent intelligent sampling techniques. The results show that traditional static sampling provides fixed, rule-based inspection schemes that ensure comparability and compliance but lack responsiveness to process variations. Adaptive sampling introduces flexibility, allowing measurement density to be adjusted based on detected drift, anomalies, or statistical control limits. Building on this, dynamic sampling represents a paradigm shift towards predictive, real-time decision-making driven by machine learning, risk analysis, and digital twin integration. The dynamic framework continuously assesses process uncertainties and prioritizes metrology to maximize information gain, thereby significantly reducing metrology workload without impacting yield or quality. Static, adaptive, and dynamic sampling together constitute a continuous evolution from deterministic control to self-optimizing intelligence. As semiconductor nodes move towards sub-3 nm, this intelligent sampling technology is crucial for maintaining yield, cost competitiveness, and process flexibility in autonomous, data-centric wafer fabs. © 2025 by the authors.

Title: From geometric freedom to value creation: a design-driven perspective on additive manufacturing
Affiliations: Nanchang Hangkong University, Nanchang, China; Shenzhen MSU-BIT University, Shenzhen, China
Authors with affiliations: Jiang W.-G., Nanchang Hangkong University, Nanchang, China; Wu Z.-K., Nanchang Hangkong University, Nanchang, China; Qin Q.-H., Shenzhen MSU-BIT University, Shenzhen, China
Abstract: Additive manufacturing (AM) is commonly interpreted as a geometry-enabling technology. While technically accurate, this perspective underrepresents a more fundamental transformation: the transition from manufacturing-constrained design toward value-driven engineering. In this Perspective, we argue that the central question facing the AM community is no longer “What geometries can be fabricated?” but rather “What value can be created through design?” We propose design-driven additive manufacturing (D2AM) as a paradigm in which design intent, rather than process capability, acts as the primary driver of innovation. A unified three-layer framework integrating functional intent, computational co-design, and cyber-physical execution is established to formalize D2AM. To address the fragmentation of existing evaluation approaches, we introduce the Design Value Index (DVI), a dimensionless metric that captures coupled trade-offs between performance, cost, and sustainability. The proposed D2AM framework and DVI have not yet been systematically validated across application domains; their broader applicability and practical utility therefore require application-specific validation. We further interpret D2AM through three foundational mechanisms: constraint release, coupled co-design, and value-density redistribution. Together, these mechanisms illustrate how AM can reshape the topology of engineering value landscapes rather than merely enabling complex geometries. We argue that AM does not create value directly but can expand or reshape the accessible design space, potentially enabling access to higher-value regions within the performance‑cost‑sustainability landscape. Key challenges, including validation gaps, lack of standardization, and fragmented treatment of coupled trade-offs, are critically examined. We also outline a roadmap toward autonomous, data-driven design ecosystems, including future extensions toward a dynamic and uncertainty-aware DVI using lifecycle data and, where appropriate, digital-twin-supported model updating. This Perspective positions D2AM as a foundational framework for next-generation engineering systems in which design, manufacturing, and lifecycle intelligence are deeply integrated. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Author full names: Hartung, Thomas (7005429459)
Title: Validation by design: Model-informed validation design (MIVD) as a quantitative design science
Affiliations: Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing (CAAT), Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, Baltimore, MD, United States; CAAT-Europe, University of Konstanz, Germany
Authors with affiliations: Hartung T., Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing (CAAT), Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, Baltimore, MD, United States, CAAT-Europe, University of Konstanz, Germany
Abstract: Validation underpins confidence in test methods and integrated testing strategies, yet while the methods under evaluation have been transformed, the design of validation studies remains gov-erned by convention and feasibility rather than prospective optimization. I propose model-informed validation design (MIVD), a quantitative framework that treats a validation study as a decision problem to be designed before resources are committed. This expands on our e-validation concept from 2024. Inspired by model-informed drug development, MIVD represents the pathway from target substance population and reference construct through biological and laboratory variability, analysis, and decision rules as an executable computational model, a digital validation twin. Can-didate designs are then compared by simulation using assurance, information economics, adaptive rules, and multi-objective optimization, with the aim of maximizing the probability of the correct, appropriately scoped validation decision rather than minimizing effort or maximizing the chance that a method will pass. Because reference standards are imperfect and contexts of use evolve, a validation becomes cumulative and can be updated along a lifecycle. A mean-based proxy recon-struction of the 1996-1997 EPISKIN skin corrosion validation shows how the preferred validation design shifts with the acceptance criteria, reference uncertainty, and chemical selection, while dem-onstrating that additional testing does not necessarily produce proportionately greater decision value. MIVD reframes validation from the evaluation of methods to the prospective design of the evidence by which those methods are judged.; Before a new safety test can be used, it must be checked, or validated, to show that it produces reliable and correct results. Such validation studies are expensive, because many chemicals are tested in several laboratories. Today validation studies are mostly designed based on past practice, rather than by working out in advance which experiments would settle the important questions. This article proposes a way to design validation studies deliberately. A digital twin imitates and compares different study designs before the laboratory work begins. Revisiting a skin corrosion vali­dation study done in 1996-1997, the approach shows that the amount of testing needed depends strongly on how much confidence in the results is required, how reliable the reference classifications are, and which chemicals are selected. Designing validation studies, rather than assembling them from templates, is the next step for safety science.

Title: Strategic Management Consultancy in the Age of Industry 5.0: Leveraging the Gig Economy for Business Transformation
Source title: Smart and Sustainable Gig Economy in the Industrial 5.0 Era: Engineering and Management Aspects
Affiliations: Institute of Cognitive Science, Tehran, Iran; Coventry University, Coventry, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Pourkhodabakhsh N., Institute of Cognitive Science, Tehran, Iran; Khajeh E., Coventry University, Coventry, United Kingdom
Abstract: The business world stands on the brink of a fundamental transformation—one initiated by the maturity of Industry 4.0 technologies and now rapidly advancing toward a new paradigm known as Industry 5.0. This paradigm shift redirects the focus from mere productivity to human-centricity, system resilience, and sustainable development. Such a transition, both technological and conceptual, has profound implications for knowledge-intensive sectors like management consulting. In this emerging landscape, consultants must not only be familiar with advanced technologies—such as artificial intelligence, collaborative robotics, and digital twins—but also harness them alongside human creativity to foster co-created value between humans and machines. Meanwhile, the growing prominence of the gig economy and structural shifts in the workforce have disrupted traditional collaboration models. Digital platforms have enabled the rise of global networks of freelance and interdisciplinary talent, allowing the formation of agile, project-based, and decentralized teams. This transformation signifies not only a new form of work but also a new type of organization—one that is open, hybrid, and adaptive, requiring consultants with the capacity to lead within such ecosystems. This study is designed to examine the tri-layered transformation—spanning technology, labor structures, and organizational models. It begins by analyzing the evolution of Industry 5.0 and its implications for redefining the role of consultants. It then explores the rise of open talent sourcing models and the strategic significance of flexible and gig-based workforces, assessing how these elements can be integrated into consulting practices. To provide practical insights, frameworks such as the consulting value-creation matrix, case vignettes from leading firms, and a five-stage action plan are introduced. Finally, using a scenario-based approach, the study outlines three plausible futures for the consulting industry through 2035, based on two critical uncertainties: the penetration level of Industry 5.0 technologies and the acceptance of independent labor. These scenarios, along with risk analyses, ethical considerations, and key performance indicators, offer a comprehensive perspective to industry stakeholders. Ultimately, this study aims to equip organizational leaders and consultants with the strategic, ethical, and human-centered capabilities necessary to navigate the evolving future of consulting. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Ehsan Khajeh and Zahra Mohammadnazari; individual chapters, the contributors.

Abstract: Breast cancer PAM50 subtype classification is hindered by the single-pass prediction paradigm of existing deep learning systems, which provide no mechanism for iterative representation refinement or uncertainty trajectory analysis. We present the Cross-Cohort Modality-Disjoint Latent Simulation (CDLS) framework: a closed-loop latent trajectory classification system that integrates histopathology (WSI), transcriptomics (RNA-seq), mammography sequences, and clinical covariates from three non-overlapping cohorts under a modality-disjoint regime in which no patient possesses all modalities simultaneously and learning proceeds via shared latent alignment rather than per-patient fusion. A PPO-governed stochastic policy refines the latent state z ∈ R7 across T = 5 optimisation steps through a Twin-GRU transition model; a defining feature is the closed-loop latent feedback step applied after each transition, which aligns simulated states with real patient embeddings via kNN retrieval: zt+1 = T (zt, at) + λ1/k Σi∈N(zt)(zi − zt). Multi-seed evaluation (n = 4, training stability only) yields Balanced Accuracy 0.870±0.044 and MCC 0.904±0.046; five-fold cross-validated results confirm stability (Accuracy 0.871±0.029, MCC 0.897±0.038, df = 19). An extended 8-seed analysis yields 0.872±0.029, consistent with the 4-seed result all comparative conclusions remain variance-aware (σ≈0.034). PPO is selected for its trajectory geometry properties (broader latent coverage, higher path diversity) rather than marginal accuracy gains, which fall within multi-seed variance. The dtwin = 7 bottleneck is empirically guided by intrinsic dimensionality estimates (did = 6.3±0.4); it is not claimed as a theoretically optimal value. The closed-loop latent framework terminology is used in a computational, representation-space sense only. © 2013 IEEE.
