Title: Human-Centric Job-Shop Production Planning and Scheduling System Based on the Concept of I5.0
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering, University of Engineering and Technology, Taxila, Pakistan
Authors with affiliations: Javaid W., Department of Industrial Engineering, University of Engineering and Technology, Taxila, Pakistan; Ullah S., Department of Industrial Engineering, University of Engineering and Technology, Taxila, Pakistan
Abstract: Production systems must constantly adapt to changing conditions, requiring planners to make complex decisions under uncertainty that significantly impact operational and financial performance. While digitalization of Production Planning and Scheduling (PPS) has been widely adopted using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and machine learning in Industry 4.0 (I4.0), I4.0 often overlooks human concentration and fatigue, which can compromise the robustness of production plans. Industry 5.0 (I5.0) addresses this limitation by leveraging human expertise and creativity to create intelligent, value-driven, and sustainable production systems. This study develops a Digital Twin (DT)–based PPS system for a job-shop production model, integrating Dynamic Break Integration (DBI). The framework actively involves operators via smartwatches, capturing real-time data on microbreaks, operator status, and situational awareness. By combining human feedback, dynamic break management, and automated planning, the system improves decision-making clarity, reduces fatigue, and enhances both worker welfare and productivity. Testing in a job-shop scenario demonstrated significant improvements in schedule adherence, cycle time, and overall efficiency. These results confirm that incorporating DBI and human-in-the-loop feedback into DT-based PPS enables a responsive, human-centric production environment, fully realizing the principles of I5.0 while achieving higher performance than conventional I4.0 approaches. Abstract: Most of the ocean’s life and biogeochemical activity is hidden from our satellite view, occurring in a vast vertical dimension that fundamentally governs marine ecosystems, the global carbon cycle, and Earth’s climate. For decades, oceanography from space has been limited to a 2D surface perspective, with early light detection and ranging (lidar) offering tantalizing but quantitatively flawed glimpses into the ocean’s interior. Here, we review the significant advancement driven by high-spectral-resolution lidar (HSRL), a technology that resolves this long-standing uncertainty. By directly measuring depth-resolved optical properties, HSRL transitions ocean profiling from estimation to quantitative measurement. The recent launches of the first spaceborne HSRL systems mark a major development in this new era. This technological step enables a “virtual constellation” in which HSRL provides the vertical backbone, hyperspectral sensors add biological complexity, and the Biogeochemical-Argo (BGC-Argo) network provides in situ biogeochemical context. This synergistic system is paving the way for 4D (3D space + time) ocean monitoring, providing the essential data streams to build a predictive “ocean digital twin”—a critical tool to advance our understanding of the ocean’s response to climate change and to support global efforts in sustainable development. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Modern weather forecasting: mathematical foundations, tools and current state of the art
Affiliations: “ItalianMeteo” National Agency, Bologna, Italy; Dipartimento di Matematica ed Informatica “Ulisse Dini”, Università di Firenze, Viale Morgagni 67/a, Firenze, 50134, Italy

Abstract: Modern weather forecasting relies on the integration of observational systems, numerical modeling, data assimilation, high-performance computing, and increasingly artificial intelligence techniques. This paper reviews the scientific and technological foundations of contemporary weather prediction, with particular emphasis on the mathematical and computational tools that support operational forecasting. Weather prediction is based on the numerical solution of the nonlinear partial differential equations governing atmospheric dynamics. The accuracy of these forecasts critically depends on the availability of observations collected from heterogeneous sources, including ground-based networks, weather radars, satellites, aircraft, and other remote sensing platforms. These data are combined with model forecasts through advanced data assimilation techniques, which provide dynamically consistent estimates of the atmospheric state and improve forecast quality. Special attention is devoted to nowcasting, one of the most challenging areas of modern meteorology. At lead times of a few minutes to several hours, rapidly evolving phenomena such as severe thunderstorms, hailstorms, and flash floods require the integration of high-frequency observations, radar extrapolation methods, ensemble prediction techniques, and machine learning approaches. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to enhance the detection, tracking, and short-term prediction of convective systems, complementing traditional physics-based methodologies. The paper also discusses the requirements of a modern national forecasting system and presents the high-resolution ICON-2I modeling framework operational at the ItaliaMeteo Agency. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of high-performance computing infrastructures, ensemble forecasting systems, and kilometer-scale data assimilation methods. Finally, current challenges and future developments are examined, including convective-scale prediction, uncertainty quantification, exascale computing, digital twins of the atmosphere, and the growing integration of artificial intelligence with numerical weather prediction. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Computational Sustainability for Climate-Resilient Materials: AI-Driven Decarbonization Pathways for Cement and Industrial Systems
Affiliations: Department of Electrical Power Engineering, Durban University of Technology, Durban, 4001, South Africa
Authors with affiliations: Ige O.E., Department of Electrical Power Engineering, Durban University of Technology, Durban, 4001, South Africa; Kabeya M., Department of Electrical Power Engineering, Durban University of Technology, Durban, 4001, South Africa
Abstract: Cement production remains a major industrial source of anthropogenic CO₂ because emissions arise from both limestone calcination and high-temperature fuel combustion. This review examines how computational sustainability can support climate-resilient and low-carbon cement production by integrating artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), digital twins, optimization, life cycle assessment (LCA), techno-economic analysis, and industrial systems modeling. An interdisciplinary scoping review was conducted using Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) informed procedures to synthesize evidence across materials discovery, cement and concrete mix optimization, plant operations, LCA integration, and system-level decarbonization planning. The review identifies computational sustainability as a multi-scale decision-support framework that links materials design, plant operations, supply-chain coordination, and policy/system planning. The synthesis shows that supervised learning, ensemble models, physics-informed neural networks, explainable AI, multi-objective optimization, digital twins, and system dynamics can support low-carbon binder screening, SCM optimization, kiln control, predictive maintenance, environmental-impact assessment, and infrastructure planning. SCM-based clinker substitution and energy-efficiency improvements are the most mature near-term options, while alternative binders, electrification, hydrogen integration, and cement-specific carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) require further validation, cost reduction, infrastructure development, and alignment with standards. Critical gaps remain in open and representative datasets, external model validation, uncertainty quantification, long-term durability evidence, multi-plant field trials, and integrated prospective LCA–techno-economic–system modeling. The review concludes that computational sustainability can accelerate cement-sector decarbonization when data-driven prediction, physical constraints, environmental assessment, economic evaluation, and policy-aware systems planning are integrated into transparent and validated decision frameworks. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Treatment response assessment and prediction

Abstract: Evaluating the efficacy of treatment, monitoring the response of cancer and normal tissue to combinations of localized radiation and systemic agents, and predicting the biological dynamics of specific patients and lesions have grown increasingly sophisticated. This progress is driven by the large-scale mining of medical imaging (DICOM PACS) and radiation oncology (DICOM RT PACS) data sources, which power the learning of AI analytical platforms. In this chapter, we will delve into image-based and AI-assisted in oncology. We will first the current clinical standards for assessing treatment response using various medical imaging modalities. We will then present a literature of treatment response assessment and prediction at various spatial scales (patient level, lesion/organ level, and voxel level) with evaluations at key timepoints: pre-, mid/during-, and post-treatment, as well as longitudinally over multiple timepoints. Our primary focus will be on cancer responses, with additional considerations for normal tissue dose-responses. We will examine data-driven approaches to treatment response and outcome prediction, including classical machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models. We will highlight strengths and limitations of prediction modeling and the need for model explainability and uncertainty quantification. Finally, we will explore future directions in treatment response assessment and offer perspectives on integrating multi-omics data, complementing biophysical and empirical models, leveraging multi-task and multi-modal frameworks, and investing in digital twin technologies for personalized oncology. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Xiaofeng Yang and Tonghe Wang; individual chapters, the contributors.

Abstract: Humans can navigate an unfamiliar city and gradually form a coherent spatial mental map spanning tens of square kilometers. Can AI build spatial representations at a comparable scale? Although recent foundation models have advanced scene reconstruction and embodied intelligence, scaling to entire cities remains an open challenge, primarily due to the lack of city-scale data. To bridge the gap, we introduce WildCity, a real-world multimodal dataset collected by autonomous fleets traversing complex urban environments. Our dataset includes 18 trajectories, each averaging 83.7 km in length, and preserves the core challenges of in-the-wild perception, e.g., dynamic objects, lighting variations, and imperfect camera poses. We further establish an urban-tailored reconstruction baseline and convert the reconstructed environments into a closed-loop simulator. Beyond the dataset and baseline, we systematically analyze the key challenges on the path to simulation-ready urban digital twins: scalability, extrapolation, and uncertainty. Ultimately, WildCity aims to catalyze progress not only in city-scale rendering, but more broadly in the pursuit of AI that can perceive, remember, and reason across space at a scale comparable to human cognition. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Abstract: Bio-energy systems are frequently promoted as low-carbon substitutes for fossil fuels and are closely related to SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) and SDG 13 (Climate Action). Actual environmental performance, however, is contingent on supply-chain design, choice of feedstock, set-up of the technology and local operating conditions. The life-cycle assessment (LCA) is currently the predominant scientific instrument for assessing these impacts in a comprehensive approach linked to SDG 12 Responsible Consumption and Production. Traditional LCA, however, has to deal with a variety of challenges including data scarcity, spatial and temporal variations, and the necessity to analyze several scenarios depending on changing circumstances. In recent years, some of these limitations can be mitigated by using artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques. This approach facilitates inventory data extrapolation, gap filling and estimation of the nonlinear function between process variables and environmental parameters, all leading to more dynamic and data rich assessment which reflects SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure). This review consolidates a summary of up-to-date studies on AI-enabled LCA approaches for bio-energy systems and pollution assessment methods that interface directly with sustainability evaluation. The paper describes a general description of key aspects related to bio-energy supply chains in LCAs regarding impact categories, including greenhouse gas (GHG), air pollutants, land use and water use with relevance to SDG 6-Clean Water and Sanitation and SDG 15-Life on Land. It subsequently provides an overview of AI and ML applications covering the full bio-energy life cycle, including aspects related to biomass resource assessment and feedstock production as well conversion, upgrading, refining, distribution to end use. Particular focus is given to works that integrate ML with LCA metrics for the prediction of environmental performance or for the optimization of process conditions through sustainability-based indicators. The review also presents AI-facilitated pollution monitoring applications, such as deep learning techniques for emissions detection using remote sensing data, carbon emissions prediction, and air quality monitoring through ML for betterment of SDG 11 (Sustainable Development Goals: Sustainable cities and communities). Major challenges including model interpretability, system boundary consistency, uncertainty propagation and hybrid modelling requirements have been identified. Next, AI focusing on digital twin, scenario analysis supported by AI and interactive LCA tool for informed decision making. © 2026 by author(s).

Title: HarmonE: A Self-adaptive Approach to Architecting Sustainable MLOps
Affiliations: Software Engineering Research Centre, IIIT Hyderabad, Hyderabad, India; Microsoft, Hyderabad, India
Authors with affiliations: Bhatt H., Software Engineering Research Centre, IIIT Hyderabad, Hyderabad, India; Biswas S., Software Engineering Research Centre, IIIT Hyderabad, Hyderabad, India; Rakhunathan S., Microsoft, Hyderabad, India; Vaidhyanathan K., Software Engineering Research Centre, IIIT Hyderabad, Hyderabad, India
Abstract: Machine Learning Enabled Systems (MLS) are becoming integral to real-world applications, but ensuring their sustainable performance over time remains a significant challenge. These systems operate in dynamic environments and face runtime uncertainties like data drift and model degradation, which affect the sustainability of MLS across multiple dimensions: technical, economical, environmental, and social. While Machine Learning Operations (MLOps) addresses the technical dimension by streamlining the ML model lifecycle, it overlooks other dimensions. Furthermore, some traditional practices, such as frequent retraining, incur substantial energy and computational overhead, thus amplifying sustainability concerns. To address them, we introduce HarmonE, an architectural approach that enables self-adaptive capabilities in MLOps pipelines using the MAPE-K loop. HarmonE allows system architects to define explicit sustainability goals and adaptation thresholds at design time, and performs runtime monitoring of key metrics, such as prediction accuracy, energy consumption, and data distribution shifts, to trigger appropriate adaptation strategies. We validate our approach using a Digital Twin (DT) of an Intelligent Transportation System (ITS), focusing on traffic flow prediction as our primary use case. The DT employs time series ML models to simulate real-time traffic and assess various flow scenarios. Our results show that HarmonE adapts effectively to evolving conditions while maintaining accuracy and meeting sustainability goals.  © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Abstract: Trustworthy AI in agriculture is increasingly framed around autonomy: can the system be left alone? We argue this framing is a structural mismatch for an important class of operational environments, which we name expertise-curated environments - domains characterised by expertise-as-ground-truth held by a slow-to-train expert pool, cost-asymmetric errors, and regulatory density. In such environments, autonomy-first decision-making is structurally unfit, not merely conservative to deploy. We propose Curated Uncertainty Exchange (CUE), a pattern in which the expert seeds the AI's training by curating ground truth upstream and arbitrates its operation by reconsultation on ranked uncertainty downstream, mediated by a rank-robust gate that is tolerant of imperfect confidence calibration. We instantiate CUE for heritage viticulture as a deployment pattern over the recently published vinum-Analytics pipeline for grapevine variety identification on the Vinha Maria Teresa parcel of Quinta do Crasto. We re-read vinum-Analytics' published evaluation through the CUE lens and argue that its three operationally-relevant findings - 100% Top-5 accuracy on the in-distribution test set, residual errors concentrated among morphologically similar variety pairs, and a 14.6% detection-failure rate identified as the primary deployment bottleneck - jointly motivate a two-part escalation gate (a structural abstention mechanism for upstream perception failure and a rank-percentile uncertainty mechanism for classifier uncertainty) whose combined expert-review budget is plausibly bounded at K≈15-20%, subject to validation with per-prediction confidence traces and plant-disjoint temporal data. We close by sketching how a multi-session aerial resurvey dataset, already collected at the same site and now under analysis, will support a temporal extension of the gate in future work. © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Aircraft line maintenance is essential for flight safety, regulatory compliance, and operational efficiency, particularly in the high-frequency, cost-sensitive operations of low-cost carriers (LCCs). As LCCs depend on tight schedules and minimal ground times, optimizing line maintenance during aircraft turnaround has become a critical research focus. This paper provides a systematic review of hybrid optimization approaches developed between 2005 and 2025 to enhance line maintenance scheduling and minimize turnaround time (TAT). Drawing on over 100 academic and industrial sources, the review categorizes contributions across three domains: dynamic programming, heuristic and metaheuristic methods, and machine learning driven predictive analytics. It examines how hybrid models’ combinations of algorithmic approaches have evolved to address complexity, uncertainty, and real-time demands in maintenance environments. Industrial adoption is also assessed, with attention to successful applications, scalability challenges, and limitations in LCC operations. A structured methodology was employed to select and evaluate literature by relevance, rigor, and practical implications. Key performance indicators including TAT reduction, resource utilization, task delay mitigation, and system robustness are synthesized using comparative tables and graphical summaries. The paper highlights research gaps such as limited integration with real-time control systems, underuse of reliability data, and insufficient attention to human factors. The review concludes with recommendations for integrating predictive maintenance data, reinforcement learning, and digital twin technologies into future optimization research. By consolidating fragmented knowledge, this work provides actionable insights for reducing TAT and improving maintenance decision-making in low-cost airline operations. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

Abstract: Featured Application: The results of this review are directly applicable to the design and implementation of predictive maintenance systems for next-generation satellites. Specifically, the study serves as a guide for satellite operators and aerospace engineers to move from traditional out-of-bound monitoring to hybrid data mining architectures. These architectures, particularly those that integrate digital twins and physics-based machine learning, are identified as the most effective solutions for managing telemetry uncertainty and detecting incipient failures in subsystems, such as the power supply system and the attitude determination and control system, thereby extending mission life and autonomy. Early detection of faults in artificial satellites is crucial for the success of missions, but it is hindered by the scarcity of data on faults and the limitations of traditional monitoring methods. As an alternative, technological trends such as data mining have emerged. This study presents a literature review to provide an in-depth examination of the landscape of data mining applications for early fault detection in satellites. Following the PRISMA protocol, the available scientific corpus from seven scientific databases was reviewed, and 52 primary studies were selected from an initial set of 2726 records published between 2011 and 2024. The results indicate that this is a rapidly expanding field, with an annual growth rate of 35.72%, characterized by a significant geopolitical concentration of research and funding led by China. From a methodological point of view, unsupervised approaches (~40%) predominate, a response to the lack of labeled in-flight data. However, supervised and hybrid models demonstrate superior performance, achieving F1 scores above 97% when selected or simulated data are available. A misalignment was identified in the domain, although research clearly favors the EPS due to the availability of data. Operational statistics, however, confirm that the ADCS system is the primary cause of mission failure. It is essential to note that the limited availability of public datasets and models, with less than 15% of studies providing access, is the main obstacle to reproducibility and progress. The primary conclusion of this work is that the field is expanding, and all stakeholders must contribute to its continued growth. Key actions include establishing public benchmarks that enable transparent evaluation, exploring physics-based models that account for uncertainty to address data scarcity, and concerted efforts to bridge the transfer gap from academic satellite operations to the real world. © 2026 by the authors.

Abstract: This paper recasts the grid metaverse as an operating protocol, not as a collection of visualization technologies. The proposed protocol begins with an event claim, binds the claim to asset-level evidence, selects a task model, exposes uncertainty to the operator, and records the approved response together with post-action verification. A compact state package is used to join electrical measurements, spatial relations, weather exposure, inspection evidence, maintenance status, and data confidence. Four task modules - inspection triage, renewable ramp assessment, hazard localization, and carbon-record checking - share the same execution logic but use different evidence gates and performance measures. Rather than repeating a broad technology survey, the paper contrasts database-indexed research streams by the operational link each stream leaves unresolved. The resulting framework is evaluated as a protocol through baseline comparison, event replay, and staged field testing. Its principal value is a testable separation between evidence, inference, human authority, and physical feedback.  © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Dragonfly is a NASA New Frontiers mission with the goal of exploring Saturn’s moon Titan in the mid-2030s using an autonomous relocatable rotorcraft lander. Titan’s low gravity (approximately 1/7th Earth’s) and dense atmosphere (approximately 4 times Earth’s) provide some of the most energy-efficient conditions in the Solar System for rotorcraft flight. However, these same factors prevent flight testing a Titan rotorcraft on Earth prior to launch. As a result, modeling and simulation underpin the design and analysis of Dragonfly to a much greater degree than they do for terrestrial rotorcraft. To that end, this paper describes the Mobility Closed-Loop Simulation, a high-fidelity parametric digital twin for modeling RPM-controlled multirotors, and its application to the prediction of Dragonfly’s flight performance at Titan. The results emphasize several fundamental differences between rotorcraft flight on Earth and Titan, including (i) how Titan’s high atmospheric density results in low rotor induced velocities that constrain the size of Dragonfly’s flight envelope in descent, and (ii) how robustness to environmental uncertainties often comes at the cost of aerodynamic efficiency. © 2025, American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics Inc, AIAA. Title: Fine-Tuning and Deployment of a Vision-Language-Action Based Robotic Foundation Model for Open-Source Robot Arms
Source title: ICHORA 2026 - 8th International Congress on Human-Computer Interaction, Optimization and Robotic Applications, Proceedings
Affiliations: Kocaeli University, Information Systems Engineering Department, Kocaeli, Turkey; Hisar Saǧlik R&d Center, Istanbul, Turkey

Abstract: This paper presents an end-to-end robotic infrastructure for deploying vision-language-action (VLA) models on the open-source BCN3D Moveo robot arm. The approach combines a ROS2-based real-time control stack, a high-fidelity digital twin in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, a LeRobot-formatted dataset converted from RLDS, and efficient fine-tuning strategies for the GROOT 1.5 foundation model. The proposed framework targets low-cost manipulation with a single RGB camera while addressing sim-to-real transfer, generalization to unseen objects, and data scarcity. Experimental evaluation reports a 60% task success rate (95% CI: $38.7\%-78.1 \%$) on the selected manipulation setup, with most failures stemming from pre-grasp alignment uncertainty and partial visual occlusion. An ablation study over training data volume (39 vs. 47 episodes) and fine-tuning epoch depth shows that richer task variation shifts the optimal checkpoint from mid- to late-stage training, yielding a 7.8 % improvement in offline MSE. Comparative fine-tuning experiments further reveal that backbone LoRA training for GR00T and $\pi_{0}$ is blocked by HuggingFace Transformers incompatibilities, while OpenVLA full fine-tuning fails due to out-of-memory constraints. Offline action-space error analysis reports MSE, RMSE, and MAE values of $0.1073,0.3275$, and 0.1523, respectively.  © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: The growing complexity of, and demand from, modern supply chains, coupled with technological advancements, have enabled the advent of smart warehouses. In these infrastructures, several technological advancements, such as: automation, robotics, simulation, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Internet of Things (IoT) devices; are employed to enhance operational performance. This work details a structured literature review, focused on smart warehouses, uncovering the role of discrete-event simulation (DES) in that domain. Particularly, in the development and optimization of smart warehouses. Moreover, it is explored how data integration, and its structuring, is critical to smart warehouses, and how it all can enable the contribution of simulation, supporting informed decision-making. The review covers key areas, including the historical evolution of warehouse systems, past scientific links between simulation and warehouse systems, the integration of AI on smart warehouses, Digital Twins of smart warehouses, the sustainability of smart warehouses, and the challenges to their implementation, such as high implementation costs, technical integration difficulties, and organization challenges. The findings highlight the strategic value of simulation in supporting the transition to more adaptive, intelligent warehouse systems, testing operational scenarios, and managing uncertainty. This paper concludes by identifying research opportunities that focus on scalable data-driven approaches to simulation. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: Strategic prioritization framework of circular battery lifecycle strategies in India’s battery-as-a-Service (BaaS): an integrated multi-method empirical analysis in India’s electric vehicle ecosystem
Affiliations: Vinod Gupta School of Management, Indian Institute of Technology, West Bengal, Kharagpur, 721302, India
Authors with affiliations: Haldar U., Vinod Gupta School of Management, Indian Institute of Technology, West Bengal, Kharagpur, 721302, India; Pradhan R.P., Vinod Gupta School of Management, Indian Institute of Technology, West Bengal, Kharagpur, 721302, India; Chandra H., Vinod Gupta School of Management, Indian Institute of Technology, West Bengal, Kharagpur, 721302, India
Abstract: Electric vehicles (EVs) are central to transport decarbonization, yet lithium-ion batteries pose major sustainability challenges across extraction, manufacturing, use, and end-of-life stages. Battery-as-a-Service (BaaS) offers a promising pathway to operationalize circular economy principles by decoupling battery ownership from vehicle ownership and embedding lifecycle responsibility within service providers. However, strategic prioritization of circular lifecycle interventions remains fragmented and weakly theorized, particularly for emerging EV ecosystems characterized by regulatory volatility, technological heterogeneity, and market uncertainty. This study develops and empirically applies an integrated Fuzzy Delphi–Best Worst Method (BWM)–Fuzzy DEMATEL framework to identify, prioritize, and structurally analyze critical battery lifecycle strategies supporting circular BaaS implementation in India. Fuzzy Delphi is employed to establish construct validity and expert consensus under epistemic uncertainty, BWM to derive parsimonious and high-consistency priority weights, and Fuzzy DEMATEL to reveal causal interdependencies and feedback structures among the shortlisted strategies. Based on inputs from 55 cross-sectoral experts spanning industry, policy, and academia, nine critical strategies are retained from an initial pool of thirty. Results indicate that battery takeback schemes, AI-driven lifecycle management, and end-of-lease recovery programs represent dominant driving strategies, while predictive maintenance and digital twin tracking function primarily as dependent enablers whose effectiveness is conditioned by higher-order system capabilities. Methodologically, the study contributes a unified uncertainty-handling decision pipeline integrating consensus formation, consistency-optimized weighting, and causal mapping. Practically, it translates analytical outputs into actionable sequencing rules and governance priorities for circular BaaS ecosystems. The framework offers transferable decision support for policymakers and industry actors seeking to structure circular battery governance in emerging and developed EV markets. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Operational Research Society of India 2026.

Title: AI and fuzzy logic in traffic accident prediction and prevention
Source title: Artificial Intelligence and Fuzzy Logic for Next-Generation Intelligent Transportation Systems
Affiliations: Computer Science & Technology, American International University West Africa, Serekunda, Gambia
Authors with affiliations: Fabiyi O., Computer Science & Technology, American International University West Africa, Serekunda, Gambia; Olanipekun W., Computer Science & Technology, American International University West Africa, Serekunda, Gambia
Abstract: Road traffic accidents represent an acute global issue, with approximately 1.19 million fatalities annually, demanding innovative solutions beyond traditional statistical approaches like Poisson and Negative Binomial regression models. This study presents a comprehensive theoretical framework that synergizes Artificial Intelligence (AI), fuzzy logic, and Systemic Safety Science through the Haddon Matrix to revolutionize accident prediction and prevention strategies. The study proposes a framework that employs advanced AI techniques, including Bayesian Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for temporal risk assessment, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for spatial relationship modeling, and XGBoost for feature importance analysis, which can process diverse data sources such as traffic patterns, weather conditions, and vehicle telemetry. Complementing these AI components, the chapter proposes a Mamdani-type fuzzy inference system that can translate predictive outputs into actionable safety measures like adaptive speed controls and collision warnings, effectively handling real-world uncertainties through interpretable linguistic rules. The Haddon Matrix provides the structural foundation, systematically organizing interventions across host (driver-related), agent (vehicle-related), and environmental factors throughout pre-crash, crash, and post-crash phases. The proposed MATLAB/Simulink-based implementation architecture incorporates data pipelines from Kaggle and HighD datasets, hybrid AI-fuzzy decision modules, and continuous feedback mechanisms for model refinement at five-second intervals. Notable innovations include enhanced explainability through Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) techniques, adaptive learning capabilities for evolving traffic scenarios, and compliance with ISO 26262/5469 safety standards. While the framework demonstrates significant theoretical promise for intelligent transportation systems, it acknowledges practical challenges, including data privacy concerns, sensor reliability issues, and stringent real-time processing requirements with sub-500ms latency thresholds. Future research directions highlight the potential of edge computing, digital twin technology, and regulatory sandbox environments to bridge the gap between theoretical conception and practical deployment, ultimately aiming to create safer, more responsive transportation ecosystems that harmonize computational precision with a human-centric control paradigm. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Mariya Ouaissa, Mariyam Ouaissa, Najib Ben Aoun, Anass Cherrafi, Rahul Kar; individual chapters, the contributors.

Title: Machine learning-enabled wastewater-based surveillance for emerging pathogen detection and monitoring: current applications, challenges, and future prospects

Abstract: Wastewater-based surveillance (WBS) has become an important public-health tool for tracking community-level circulation of emerging and re-emerging pathogens, but wastewater measurements are not directly interpretable public-health indicators. Signals recovered from sewer systems are shaped by sampling variability, environmental and inter- and intra-laboratory variations, population-dependent bias, and high-dimensional molecular complexity. Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used to extract predictive and decision-relevant information from these data, but the strength of the supporting evidence varies substantially. This narrative review examines how strongly current applications are supported by published evidence. Sources were identified through iterative searches of three literature-search sources updated to June 2026 and classified by role, analytical task, and strength of evidence. To keep the analytical scope consistent, we use a pragmatic four-layer classification: classical statistical models, conventional machine learning, deep learning, and hybrid or mechanistically informed approaches. Applications are reviewed across five analytical tasks: predictive modelling and forecasting, anomaly and fluctuation detection, data harmonization and normalization, high-dimensional interpretation, and integrated decision support. Among 35 sources reporting analytical or modelling work, 25 analyzed SARS-CoV-2 alone; demonstrated early-warning evidence came predominantly from L1 methods, and most target–task combinations remain prospective. Even within SARS-CoV-2 surveillance, reported performance was context-dependent. We examine the data-quality, methodological, and implementation barriers that limit broader application and validation. Future priorities include standardized and collaborative frameworks, multimodal data fusion, mechanistic and digital-twin modelling with explicit uncertainty assessment, and transparent and actionable analytics, with broader surveillance applications constrained by governance and public acceptability. © 2026 The Author(s). Abstract: The inverse Finite Element Method (iFEM) is a robust and efficient computational technique for reconstructing full-field displacements from strain measurements, requiring only structural geometry, boundary conditions, and sensor data—without the need for material properties or external load information. While its independence from loading conditions makes it particularly suitable for aerospace Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) and Digital Twin (DT) frameworks, three major challenges limit its application to aerospace composite structures: (i) most existing studies focus on simplified structural configurations rather than realistic, full-scale assemblies, (ii) sparse sensor layouts, which reduce reconstruction accuracy, and (iii) uncertainty or degradation of boundary conditions, which can significantly compromise shape sensing performance. This study presents a novel combined numerical–experimental methodology for advanced shape sensing of a full-scale composite Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) stabilizer under non-ideal boundary conditions. The approach integrates Smoothing Element Analysis (SEA) into the iFEM framework to pre-extrapolate strain fields from limited sensor measurements. Given the structural complexity of the stabilizer, SEA is applied on different planes of the structure, starting from instrumented areas and progressively extending to non-instrumented regions. Furthermore, the methodology explicitly accounts for non-ideal boundary constraints arising from joint loosening and support compliance. The methodology is experimentally validated on a full-scale composite stabilizer equipped with a LUNA distributed fiber optic sensor network, with reconstruction accuracy assessed under various ideal and non-ideal support configurations. Several experimental tests are performed in which the stabilizer is subjected to two external forces, inducing bending and torsion in a cantilever beam configuration. Results show that, when only ideal boundary conditions are assumed, displacement reconstruction errors can exceed 14 % at key measurement points, which is not acceptable for SHM purposes. By explicitly modeling joint loosening and support compliance, reconstruction errors are reduced to approximately 2 %, achieving the accuracy required for real-world applications. These findings highlight the potential of the proposed SEA–iFEM approach for real-time monitoring of complex composite aircraft structures in realistic operational scenarios, where non-ideal boundary conditions cannot be neglected. © 2025 The Author(s).

Title: Applications of reactor produced radioisotopes for radioactive particle tracking (RPT) studies in various multiphase process columns

Abstract: Multiphase process columns, including fluidized beds, risers and downers, bubble columns, slurry and trickle-bed reactors, and three-phase contactors, are widely used in catalytic cracking, combustion, gasification, and chemical synthesis. Their internal hydrodynamics remain difficult to characterize because these systems are opaque, densely loaded, and often operate under harsh conditions. Radioactive particle tracking (RPT) overcomes these limitations by tracking the three-dimensional Lagrangian motion of a gamma-emitting tracer particle using an external array of scintillation detectors, enabling non-invasive measurement of particle trajectories, velocity fields, residence-time distributions, dispersion coefficients, granular temperature, and mixing characteristics. This review covers reactor-produced radioisotopes, including production routes, nuclear and physical characteristics (gamma energy, emission yield, half-life, chemical compatibility), isotope-selection criteria, and tracer/particle preparation, along with the radioisotope-RPT linkage that remains under addressed despite being fundamental to measurement accuracy. It then details RPT methodology, including detector systems, particle-localization and trajectory-reconstruction algorithms, and the hydrodynamic parameters derivable from tracked trajectories, such as velocity and turbulence statistics, solids/liquid holdup, circulation patterns, dispersion coefficients, and residence-time distributions, along with sources of uncertainty. Applications across gas–solid, gas–liquid, liquid–solid, and gas–liquid-solid columns are synthesized to compare reactor configurations, identify hydrodynamic consensus and contradictions, and examine RPT's role in validating CFD/DEM models against complementary diagnostics such as PEPT, gamma-ray CT, and gamma-scanning densitometry. Current limitations in detector calibration and isotope logistics are discussed alongside emerging opportunities in machine-learning-assisted reconstruction and digital-twin integration. © Akadémiai Kiadó Zrt 2026.

Title: Getting “sampling” right for reliable process monitoring: main challenges and solutions

Abstract: In modern scientific and industrial environments, processes are increasingly monitored through dense networks of sensors generating high-dimensional and often, continuous data streams. Process Analytical Technology (PAT), originally developed in the pharmaceutical industry but now widely applied across biotechnology, food production, environmental monitoring, cultural heritage preservation, and healthcare, provides an empowering framework with which to link real-time measurements to critical quality attributes and process parameters, enabling optimal process understanding, control, and optimization. Despite continuing, impressive advances in sensor technology and chemometric modelling, a persistent misconception is that data quantity alone ensures representativity and model reliability. While data quality is important, remaining a critical success factor for PAT, material heterogeneity, sensor placement, sampling frequency, and process sampling interface design together determine how well observed process data variability and the collected data reflect the true system variability without being unduly compromised by the total measurement system errors and uncertainties. This article emphasizes the central role of the Theory of Sampling (TOS) in ensuring representative increment, sample and data acquisition, illustrating the most common sampling pitfalls including over-reliance on data augmentation, poor field-of-view selection, and neglect of temporal dynamics and demonstrates how these factors impact chemometric models across diverse applications. Emerging approaches, such as automated adaptive sampling and digital twins, offer potential to optimize data collection, but their effectiveness still relies fundamentally on informative primary sensors, which must be TOS-compliant, no exceptions. Through article reviews and examples including Raman and near infrared datasets from materials like rocks, coffee, and beer fermentation, we highlight practical strategies for integrating sampling design with sensor deployment. Overall, this study emphasizes the critical need to prioritize representative sampling, as advanced sensor technology and powerful data modelling cannot alone compensate for systematic measurement system bias, thereby ensuring reliable, interpretable, and actionable process insights. Title: Opportunities, Limitations, and Future Perspectives of Food Packaging 4.0
Source title: Food Packaging 4.0: Harnessing Innovations in Digital, Physical, and Biological Sciences for Sustainable Solutions
Affiliations: Faculty of Agricultural Engineering, University of Aleppo, Aleppo, Syrian Arab Republic; Sustainable Agri Food tech Innovation & Research (SAFIR), Syrian Elite Scientists Association (SESA), Arras, France
Authors with affiliations: Hassoun A., Faculty of Agricultural Engineering, University of Aleppo, Aleppo, Syrian Arab Republic, Sustainable Agri Food tech Innovation & Research (SAFIR), Syrian Elite Scientists Association (SESA), Arras, France
Abstract: Food Packaging 4.0 represents a paradigm shift in packaging systems, driven by the integration of Industry 4.0 technologies that transform packaging from a passive containment solution into an intelligent, connected, and data-enabled component of the food supply chain. This chapter examines the opportunities, limitations, and future perspectives of Food Packaging 4.0, with a focus on key enabling technologies, including artificial intelligence, big data analytics, blockchain, the Internet of Things and smart sensors, robotics, nanotechnology, digital twins, additive manufacturing, and augmented and immersive interfaces. These technologies offer significant potential to enhance food safety, real-time quality monitoring, traceability, operational efficiency, and sustainability, while reducing food waste and strengthening consumer trust. However, their large-scale adoption remains constrained by technical challenges related to, for example, data quality, interoperability, and scalability, as well as economic barriers, regulatory uncertainty, safety concerns, and variable consumer acceptance. By synthesizing recent advances and identifying persistent gaps, this chapter highlights critical considerations for the responsible and effective implementation of Food Packaging 4.0, paving the way for more human-centric, transparent, and resilient packaging strategies in the emerging context of Food Packaging 5.0.s © 2027 selection and editorial matter, Abdo Hassoun; individual chapters, the contributors.

Title: Fair and Safe EV Charging Under Renewable Variability: Multi-objective Scheduling with V2G

Abstract: We address city-scale fair and safe EV charging under renewable variability with bidirectional V2G. We model the city as two coupled graphs—traffic and distribution grid—and propose a hierarchical scheduler that operates in a receding-horizon loop. The upper OPF layer produces station power envelopes that are feasible with respect to feeder thermal limits, voltages, and transformer aging; the lower mobility–charging layer assigns sessions, regulates charging/V2G within envelopes, and enforces queue-aware QoS and fairness (SoC satisfaction, waiting, detours) using α-fair or lexicographic allocations. Uncertainty in renewables and arrivals is handled via robust budgets, chance constraints, and scenario sampling. The design exposes operator knobs (objective weights, risk levels, robust budgets) and requires only envelope/dual exchange, preserving privacy. In a city digital twin with 24 stations across 5 feeders (PV share ≈ 40%), our method improves safety and user experience versus Greedy/Valley-only/Grid-only baselines: peak loading 0.86 p.u. (vs 0.98/0.93/0.88), voltage violations 0.06 feeder-h/day (vs 0.42/0.21/0.09), and curtailment 3.82 MWh (vs 4.97/4.35). User metrics also improve: avg. wait 11.30 min, CVaR90_{90}90 17.20 min, Gini (wait) 0.22 (from 0.31), and SoC shortfall 2.60 p.p. (from 4.20 p.p.). Carbon is −6.8% versus Grid-only. Disabling V2G raises peak to 0.89 p.u. and curtailment by +0.71 MWh, confirming the value of controlled discharge during renewable-rich congested periods. Each receding-horizon step completes in <30 s on commodity hardware. © Beijing Paike Culture Commu. Co., Ltd. 2026.

Abstract: Biomass resource mappings are essential tasks for sustainable energy planning, since it offers information on the potential supply, geographical availability of resources, plant sitting, transportation opportunities and roadmap towards long term renewable energy concepts that have policy relevance. Its relevance is increasing as countries are embracing low carbon economy’s roadmaps which demand for reliable spatial quantitative estimations of forest and waste residues–based biomass potentials. Despite the significant headway, there are still some loopholes in applying remote sensing and machine learning techniques. These limitations comprise scarcity of good quality field data for model calibration, poor integration of socio–economic drivers and difficulties in representing fine–scale spatial variability that hinder accurate estimate of yields at different spatial levels. This paper surveys recent machine learning methods for AGB estimation, discusses their methodological limitations, and proposes future research avenues toward scalable and robust forest biomass mapping. A combination of satellite observations, GIS–based layers and ground inventory data sets are included in the analysis as well as a variety of regression, tree based, kernel based, neural network, deep learning and hybrid modelling approaches over various land coverage areas. According to the previous works, evidence is gathered from the surveyed studies that ensemble and deep learning approaches can enhance prediction performance on multi–source data; GIS–machine learning integration contributes to better site selection and logistics analysis. The results also demonstrate the potential for a combined framework that exploits transfer learning approaches and digital twin methodologies to reduce prediction uncertainty, especially in low–data areas. Such information could help support rational decision–making activities for policymakers, planners and industry actors that consider the role of bioenergy in national energy security, climate change mitigation strategies, resource sustainability and long–term renewable energy planning. © 2026 by author(s).

Title: AI-Driven Logistics, Data Governance, and Sustainability: A Critical Analysis of India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023
Source title: The Economics of Decarbonized Transport: AI Technologies, Market Mechanisms, and Policy Innovation
Affiliations: Christ University, India
Authors with affiliations: Verma V., Christ University, India; Solanki S., Christ University, India; Pandey V.D., Christ University, India; Singh S., Christ University, India; Sinha R., Christ University, India
Abstract: This paper is a critical overview of the blowout of artificial intelligence (AI)empowered logistics, cross-border data governance, and sustainability regulation as the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) of India. It addresses the ways AI-based logistic systems (including the predictive routing or digital twins systems and emission tracking systems) rely on the smooth flow of transnational data, and how the regulatory uncertainty of the DPDP Act affects the efficiency of operations, compliance, and climate governance. The study places the Indian framework in a global frame using doctrinal analysis and comparative legal analysis against global regimes of EU GDPR, OECD Privacy Guidelines and APEC CBPR system. The results underscore a regulatory paradox: Reconciling data sovereignty, AI-trade efficiencies, and sustainability imperatives. The article posits that in order to match the global data protection law with the decarbonization and digital trade agenda in India, interoperable, risk-based, and technologically adaptive governance frameworks are necessary. Abstract: The power grid dispatch management mechanism serves as the cornerstone for balancing the multi-dimensional objectives of "safety, economy, and low-carbon"in power systems. In recent years, traditional dispatch mechanisms have faced challenges such as difficulties in managing uncertainties, low efficiency in multi-regional coordination, and insufficient security resilience, all influenced by the high proportion of renewable energy integration, diversified electricity markets, and digital technology innovations. This paper systematically reviews research progress on optimizing dispatch management mechanisms through five dimensions: technology-driven approaches, renewable energy adaptation, dispatch model innovation, security resilience assurance, and institutional policy coordination, based on 29 domestic and international studies. The research reveals that: 1) At the technical level, deep learning and artificial intelligence are core drivers for enhancing intelligent dispatch decision-making; 2) For renewable energy adaptation, dynamic spinning reserve optimization, virtual inertia control, and coordinated dispatch of energy storage and microgrids effectively address intermittency and low-inertia challenges; 3) Multi-regional dispatch overcomes the limitations of centralized systems through distributed optimization algorithms and hierarchical control architectures; 4) Security resilience relies on coordinated smart operations, cybersecurity protection, and emergency dispatch strategies; 5) The transmission-distribution integration framework and incentive policies provide crucial institutional support for these optimizations. Finally, the paper summarizes challenges in data robustness, technological resilience, and institutional coordination, while outlining future directions including deep integration of "AI + digital twin"systems, multi-stakeholder collaboration, and resilience-oriented policy innovation.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Application of digital modeling tools for the design and development of infrastructure facilities in the extractive industry; [Применение инструментов цифрового моделирования для проектирования и развития объектов инфраструктуры добывающих активов]

Authors with affiliations: Savelyev S.V., LUKOIL-Engineering LLC, Moscow, Russian Federation
Abstract: This paper presents a methodological approach to pre-investment and conceptual design of infrastructure for production assets based on an integrated digital model. The relevance of the study is driven by high uncertainty in initial data during early development stages, the need for coordinated consideration of production dynamics, hydraulic constraints, power supply parameters, spatial positioning of facilities, and technical-economic criteria. A sequential process is proposed for developing a spatiotemporal asset model, simulating production gathering and transportation networks, electrical grids, and conducting multi-scenario comparison of development concepts. The methodology was tested on an asset comprising several separate fields unified under common infrastructure. It is demonstrated that when final geological targets for production drilling are not yet defined, the digital model enables estimation of projected production levels, locations of gathering centers, pipeline routes and diameters, as well as options for placement of processing facilities. Based on calculation results, a scheme was justified involving construction of a central processing facility at licence block (LB) LB-2; installation of a DN 250 oil pipeline connecting to an existing field; and connection of LU-3 via a DN 250 pipeline in 2051. Integration of engineering calculations with financial-economic models enables creation of a decision tree and elimination of technologically unfeasible or economically inefficient alternatives. © 2026, Neftyanoe Khozyaistvo. Abstract: The complicated issues that policymakers and researchers face are explored in this chapter, along with new developments and trends in modeling sustainable environmental systems. Integrated frameworks that capture complex interactions among ecological processes, climatic trends, human activity, and policy interventions have replaced isolated domain-specific approaches in environmental system modeling. Multiscale models that successfully connect macro-level environmental changes with micro-level ecological processes have been the focus of recent developments, offering a more thorough comprehension of system behavior across temporal and geographical dimensions. Traditional physics-based models have been combined with artificial intelligence and machine learning to improve predictive skills while controlling computational complexity, particularly when dealing with complicated feedback systems and heterogeneous input sources. By integrating many stakeholder viewpoints into the model-building process, participatory modeling techniques have grown in popularity and have enhanced modeling results and potential for implementation. These cooperative approaches have been successful in bringing disparate interest groups together and converting intricate scientific discoveries into workable policy suggestions. This chapter emphasizes how robust scenario analysis and uncertainty quantification have emerged as crucial elements of contemporary environmental modeling, facilitating more resilient decision-making in the face of socioeconomic shifts and climate variability. Furthermore, new possibilities for adaptive environmental management techniques have been made possible by the development of digital twin technologies and real-time monitoring systems. To improve our ability to navigate complex sustainability challenges, future research directions include developing standardized protocols for model validation across a variety of environmental contexts, refining methods for representing emergent system properties, and developing ethical frameworks that integrate equity considerations into model design. © 2027 selection and editorial matter, Satya Prakash Maurya, Akhilesh Kumar Yadav, Ramesh Singh, Prashant Kumar.

Abstract: The implementation of hydrogen (H2) in transportation, industrial applications, and energy systems underscores the importance of explosion risk management, particularly for H2–air and hybrid mixtures (including hydrocarbon and particulate/metal additives). This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of (i) theoretical and computational methodologies: 0D/1D screening, 1D flame acceleration/deflagration-to-detonation transition models, and 2D/3D computational fluid dynamics (Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes/large eddy simulation), with detailed versus simplified kinetics critically evaluating assumptions, accuracy constraints, and validation requirements; (ii) experimental techniques (shock tubes, detonation chambers, vented enclosures, obstructed channels) and diagnostic tools (pressure arrays, high-speed imaging, laser methodologies), encompassing scaling relationships for ignition sensitivity, flame velocity, and overpressure alongside the corresponding uncertainty/repeatability factors; and (iii) material compatibility, underscoring H2 embrittlement, permeation, fatigue, and mitigation strategies through coatings, liners, and qualification assessments. Codes and standards pertinent to design and operation (e.g. ISO 14687, ISO/TR 15916, NFPA 2, IEC 60079) are correlated with hazard controls, and application domains are delineated utilizing a technology readiness level/safety maturity perspective. Insights from significant incidents are synthesized through a cause–barrier–learning framework for prevention. Ultimately, a gap-structured roadmap prioritizes benchmark datasets, uncertainty–quantification–aware modeling, resilient sensing technologies, and auditable AI/digital twin instruments to enhance safety in H2 energy systems. © The Author(s) 2026. Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into food processing and packaging is redefining operational paradigms across the global food industry. This chapter critically examines the applications, benefits, and challenges associated with AI technologies, particularly machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, robotics, and the Internet of Things (IoT), in transforming conventional food systems into intelligent, data-driven ecosystems. AI enables real-time process optimization, predictive maintenance, non-destructive quality assessment, and dynamic shelf-life estimation, all of which contribute to improved safety, efficiency, and product consistency. In packaging, AI empowers smart systems that respond to environmental changes, enhance traceability, and facilitate consumer interaction via intelligent labeling and digital twins. Case studies from multinational food and beverage companies illustrate measurable improvements in yield, waste reduction, and compliance. The chapter also explores AI's role in supporting circular economy practices by valorizing food byproducts and optimizing resource usage. Despite these advancements, barriers such as data interoperability, cybersecurity, regulatory uncertainty, and limited adoption among small- and medium-sized enterprises persist. Ethical concerns regarding transparency, algorithmic bias, and workforce displacement are also addressed. Looking ahead, the convergence of AI with blockchain, edge computing, and advanced sensor technologies promises to further enhance the agility, sustainability, and resilience of food systems. This chapter provides a holistic perspective on how AI is not only enabling innovation in food processing and packaging but also laying the foundation for smarter, safer, and more sustainable food value chains. © 2027 selection and editorial matter, Tanmay Sarkar and Jay Kumar Pandey; individual chapters, the contributors.

Title: Seismic Failure Mechanism Shift in RC Buildings Revealed by NDT-Supported, Field-Calibrated BIM-Based Models
Affiliations: Department of Civil Engineering, Malatya Turgut Özal University, Malatya, 44210, Turkey
Authors with affiliations: Eren M.E., Department of Civil Engineering, Malatya Turgut Özal University, Malatya, 44210, Turkey; Fenerli C., Department of Civil Engineering, Malatya Turgut Özal University, Malatya, 44210, Turkey
Abstract: This study proposes a field-calibrated, NDT-integrated BIM modeling framework to improve the reliability of post-earthquake assessment for reinforced concrete (RC) buildings. The approach combines destructive and nondestructive testing (NDT) data—including core drilling, Schmidt hammer, ultrasonic pulse velocity (UPV), and Windsor probe—through a site-specific WinSonReb regression model. The calibrated material properties (average compressive strength ≈ 18.6 MPa, CoV > 20%) were embedded into a Building Information Modeling (BIM) environment, producing an as-is, NDT-calibrated BIM model representing a Level-2 static digital twin of the structure. Nonlinear static pushover analyses performed in accordance with TBDY-2018 and ASCE 41-17 showed that the calibrated model exhibits a fundamental period of 0.85 s—approximately 18% longer than the uncalibrated BIM model. This elongation increased displacement demand and caused a shift in performance classification: while the uncalibrated model indicated Life Safety (LS), the calibrated model predicted behavior approaching Collapse Prevention (CP) in the Y direction. Furthermore, calibration reversed the predicted damage hierarchy, from ductile beam hinging to brittle column- and wall-controlled failure near elevator openings, consistent with post-event observations from the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes. These results demonstrate that integrating field-calibrated NDT data into BIM-based seismic models fundamentally alters both strength estimation and failure-mechanism prediction, reducing epistemic uncertainty and providing a more conservative basis for retrofit prioritization. Although demonstrated on a single case study, the proposed workflow offers a realistic and scalable pathway for NDT-supported seismic performance assessment of existing RC buildings. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Digital transformation in geotechnical site characterization: trends, methods, and future roadmaps
Affiliations: Department of Building and Real Estate, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong; China State Construction Engineering (Hong Kong) Limited, Hong Kong
Authors with affiliations: Hu Y., Department of Building and Real Estate, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong; Li Y.; Li H., Department of Building and Real Estate, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong; Wang J., Department of Building and Real Estate, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong; Han S., Department of Building and Real Estate, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong; Hong Z., China State Construction Engineering (Hong Kong) Limited, Hong Kong; Yuan J., China State Construction Engineering (Hong Kong) Limited, Hong Kong; Zhang M., Department of Building and Real Estate, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong
Abstract: The reliability and sustainability of civil infrastructure depend on high-resolution subsurface characterization, yet conventional site investigation is often limited by labor-intensive fieldwork and sparse measurements. This critical systematic review links the digital transformation of geological surveying to geotechnical site characterization, treating remote sensing, geophysics, and digital geological mapping as upstream evidence that constrains engineering interpretation. We synthesize how multi-source observations are converted into engineering-ready site models and decision-facing uncertainty for design and risk management. Through analyzing the intellectual structure of the field, we identify a shift toward integrated workflows that combine multi-platform sensing with physics-informed and explainable AI. We discuss where these workflows are mature enough to support engineering decisions (e.g. ground model updating, hazard screening for slopes, and construction-phase monitoring), and where they remain limited by transferability, registration errors, and validation constraints. The analysis reveals that the frontier is shifting beyond data acquisition toward four-dimensional geological digital twins that can be updated through monitoring and consumed within BIM-centered delivery. This review offers a roadmap for integrating smart sensing and AI into routine engineering practice, highlighting the necessity of explainable algorithms to ensure safety and resilience in the built environment. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Multi-Modal Urban Mobility under Uncertainty: Mode Selection Based on Dynamic Transport Parameters
Affiliations: Prince Mohammad Bin Fahd University, Al Khobar, Saudi Arabia; The University of Adelaide, Adelaide, Australia
Authors with affiliations: Muhammad S., Prince Mohammad Bin Fahd University, Al Khobar, Saudi Arabia; Mohammad N., Prince Mohammad Bin Fahd University, Al Khobar, Saudi Arabia, The University of Adelaide, Adelaide, Australia
Abstract: This paper presents a detailed model of a multi-modal transportation system that integrates various travel modes—including cars, buses, trains, and bicycles—within a unified framework. The model captures heterogeneous congestion levels, mode-specific travel speeds, and critical infrastructure such as bus stops and train stations, enabling realistic intermodal transfers. To reflect operational variability, it incorporates probabilistic elements like vehicle availability, on-time performance, and delay likelihoods across transport modes. External disruptions, including accidents and adverse weather, are also modeled to assess system resilience under real-world uncertainties. The transportation network is formalized as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), allowing for the representation of stochastic behaviors and non-deterministic route choices. System properties are specified using Probabilistic Computation Tree Logic (PCTL), and a probabilistic model checker is used to evaluate performance. A comprehensive case study demonstrates how probabilistic model checking can support the design and optimization of real-world multi-modal transportation systems by enabling informed selection of key parameters. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: Mediterranean Aquaculture in a New Era of Challenges: Digital Transformation and Precision Fish Farming
Source title: Bulletin of the European Association of Fish Pathologists
Affiliations: Institute of Marine Biology Biotechnology and Aquaculture, Hellenic Centre for Marine Research, Greece
Authors with affiliations: Papandroulakis N., Institute of Marine Biology Biotechnology and Aquaculture, Hellenic Centre for Marine Research, Greece
Abstract: Mediterranean aquaculture is a strategic component of regional food production and the blue economy, supplying high-value marine species with a comparatively lower environmental footprint to many other animal protein systems. Yet the sector is entering a period of intensified pressure. Climate change, resource constraints, rising production costs, market competition, fragmented production structures, and increasingly complex regulatory demands are reshaping the conditions under which Mediterranean fish farming operates. At the same time, conventional husbandry practices remain heavily dependent on labor-intensive routines and limited observation of biological and environmental processes in open marine systems. This paper examines how digital transformation and precision fish farming can support a more resilient, efficient, and sustainable Mediterranean aquaculture sector. After outlining the current characteristics of marine fish farming in the region, the paper discusses the main structural, environmental, and economic challenges affecting production. It then presents precision fish farming as a management paradigm based on continuous observation, reliable data collection, quantitative analysis, and timely decision-making. Key enabling technologies are reviewed, including sensor networks, cameras, Internet of Things systems, remote sensing, drones, remotely operated and autonomous underwater vehicles, automated feeding systems, artificial intelligence, decision support systems, and digital twins. The paper also highlights current application areas such as environmental monitoring, forecasting and modeling, non-invasive monitoring of fish behavior and morphology, feeding optimization, site suitability analysis, and cage inspection. Particular attention is given to barriers to adoption, including investment cost, data quality, interoperability, capacity building, cybersecurity, data ownership, and the responsible use of artificial intelligence. The central argument is that digital transformation is no longer optional for Mediterranean aquaculture: it is becoming a prerequisite for adapting production systems to environmental uncertainty, improving operational performance, and strengthening long-term sustainability. However, successful implementation will depend not only on technology availability, but also on skills development, organizational readiness, and cross-disciplinary collaboration. © 2026, European Association of Fish Pathologists e.V.. Abstract: Aluminium-waste hydrolysis is a potential route for decentralized hydrogen generation because it can use post-consumer and industrial aluminium residues while reducing dependence on continuous electricity input during the reaction. This review critically evaluates aluminium waste-based hydrogen production by linking reaction chemistry, oxide-layer passivation, reactor design, performance benchmarking, techno-economic assessment (TEA), life cycle assessment (LCA), safety, and system-level integration. Reported hydrogen yields vary because of differences in alloy composition, oxide thickness, surface pretreatment, sodium hydroxide (NaOH) concentration, temperature, reactor hydrodynamics, and gas-collection methods. Continuous-flow and heat-assisted reactors generally provide better reaction stability than simple batch reactors. Still, their scale-up remains limited by corrosion, fouling, alkaline recovery, hydrogen purification, feedstock inconsistency, and aluminium hydroxide sludge management. Reported levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH), energy return on investment (EROI), carbon dioxide (CO2) reduction, and circularity values should therefore be interpreted as condition-dependent ranges rather than universal indicators. The review also discusses machine learning (ML), digital twins, predictive monitoring, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted fuel-cell energy management as future tools for improving reactor stability and hybrid renewable integration. Key research needs include standardized reporting, uncertainty-based TEA and LCA, long-duration pilot testing, safe scale-up, closed-loop NaOH recovery, and validated utilization of byproducts. © 2026 American Institute of Chemical Engineers.

Abstract: With the continuous expansion of global transportation infrastructure and the increasing frequency of extreme climate events, the risk of instability of soft rock slopes has increased dramatically. The combined effects of complex geological structures and non-stationary hydroclimatic forcing make traditional stability analysis methods and control technologies inadequate and unreliable. Recently, numerous novel approaches for the stability analysis and control of soft rock slopes have emerged. This paper systematically reviews these approaches and their core advances. The mechanical behaviour and degradation mechanisms of soft rocks are reviewed within a coupled multiphysics framework, covering soft rock classification, typical characteristics, transient and time-dependent responses, deformation behaviour and constitutive characterization and parameter evolution. The effects of individual and coupled environmental factors on rock degradation are elucidated. Secondly, stability analysis methods for soft rock slopes are reviewed, incorporating both conventional approaches and their recent advances. The improved methodologies encompass theoretical advances in (1) limit-equilibrium and block-kinematic formulations; (2) numerical modelling across continuum, discontinuum and multiscale frameworks; (3) reliability-based analyses integrating probabilistic, spatial- and time-dependent uncertainties; and (4) intelligent approaches that couple data-driven techniques with physical modelling. Reinforcement and protection technologies are subsequently reviewed, including conventional measures for rock/soil slope stabilization, as well as structural reinforcement, seepage control and ecological stabilization approaches specifically for soft rock slopes. Finally, this paper outlines future perspectives, including coupling multiphysics modelling with multi-source intelligent monitoring; advancing nature-based protection and durable protective materials; and integrating these into digital-twin platforms for dynamic reliability assessment and AI-assisted decision optimization in soft rock slope management. © The Author(s) 2026. Title: Autonomous Multi-Agent Coordination for Dynamic Construction Project Scheduling Under Resource Constraints and Environmental Uncertainties
Affiliations: Construction Project Management, University of Portsmouth, London, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Sepehri M., Construction Project Management, University of Portsmouth, London, United Kingdom
Abstract: The research proposes a new autonomous multi-agent framework that combines distributed AI algorithms and real-time construction project data to support scheduling decisions in a complex constraint environment. The framework employs a blockchain-based coordination protocol that enables reinforcement learning agents to adapt schedules and allocate resources dynamically, requiring only supervisory human oversight for exception handling. The framework was validated in a digital twin simulation environment parameterized from 47 completed construction projects using historical project data, supplemented by a prospective six-project pilot deployment to assess real-world feasibility. From the implementation, project delays have reduced by 34% and resource utilization efficiency improved by 28%. The methodology integrates stochastic modeling of weather, the supply chain, and labor into the decision-making process. Each agent specializes in domains such as materials procurement, equipment scheduling, and quality control. The architecture makes use of federated learning principles that help maintain data privacy and allow collective intelligence across project sites. The results of validation indicate major improvements in cost-performance indices and schedule variance. The framework provides real-time adaptive scheduling solutions to unexpected site challenges, addressing a critical gap in current construction management practice. Copyright © 2026 Mehran Sepehri. Affiliations: Amity Business School, Amity University, Chhattisgarh, Raipur, India; ISBM University, Chhattisgarh, Raipur, India; Symbiosis Centre for Management Studies, Symbiosis International (Deemed University), Bengaluru campus, Pune, India
