Abstract: Seismic exploration is a key geophysical method for resource exploration and development, geohazard monitoring, underground-space engineering, CO2 geological storage, geothermal energy, and subsurface energy storage. With the rapid development of wide-azimuth, broadband, high-density, nodal, and distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) acquisition, seismic data volumes are increasing rapidly, whereas high-quality labels and reliable prior knowledge remain limited. Conventional workflows that rely heavily on manual experience and serial processing therefore face substantial challenges in efficiency, stability, reproducibility, and cross-area transfer. This review aims to summarize the research status and development trends of intelligent seismic exploration from the viewpoint of the complete seismic workflow. On the basis of representative studies, public datasets, and engineering applications, we review recent progress in four main directions: intelligent acquisition, data processing and reconstruction, automated interpretation and knowledge representation, and intelligent inversion and parameter characterization. The analysis shows that self-supervised and weakly supervised learning, diffusion models, implicit representations, Transformers, large-scale pretraining, physics-informed learning, differentiable simulation, and uncertainty assessment are reshaping seismic quality control, noise attenuation, interpolation, imaging, inversion, fault and horizon interpretation, and reservoir prediction. The review further compares alternative technical routes and organizes deployment-oriented evaluation metrics in terms of data fidelity, geological consistency, target-domain validity, and engineering deployability. Finally, future trends are discussed from the perspectives of computing power, physical consistency and interpretability, cross-scale multiphysics integration, and closed-loop digital twins, with the aim of providing a methodological reference for field applications and future research in intelligent seismic exploration. © The Editorial Department of APPLIED GEOPHYSICS 2026.

Title: A Review on Integration of AI and IoT in Geotechnical Engineering
Source title: Applications of AI and IoT in Geotechnical Engineering for Sustainable Infrastructure
Affiliations: Department of Civil Engineering, Mepco Schlenk Engineering College, Tamil Nadu, Sivakasi, India; Centre for Advanced Research in Environment, School of Civil Engineering, SASTRA Deemed University, Tamil Nadu, Thanjavur, India
Authors with affiliations: Kannan G., Department of Civil Engineering, Mepco Schlenk Engineering College, Tamil Nadu, Sivakasi, India; Sujatha E.R., Centre for Advanced Research in Environment, School of Civil Engineering, SASTRA Deemed University, Tamil Nadu, Thanjavur, India
Abstract: The uncertainty in geotechnical systems and the complexity involved mandate the need for progressive approaches that are continuing in nature for areas like decision-making, analysis and monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT) offer a transformative framework to address the abovementioned areas of concern as they permit continuous real-time acquisition of geotechnical data using IoT and facilitate its integration using AI for intelligent interpretation, pattern recognition and risk forecasting using a wide range of AI techniques, including machine learning models and hybrid predictive models. Several geotechnical applications such as slope stability assessment, early warning systems, tunnel operations and performance monitoring of structures and substructures like dams, bridges and foundations using integrated AI and IoT techniques have shown considerable success. For example, parameters such as pore pressure, vibration, soil moisture and deformation/settlement are collected using a distributed sensor network and are integrated by applying predictive models to develop early warning systems for natural hazards like floods and landslides or to assess slope stability for large-scale infrastructure and developmental projects. The AI–IoT framework helps in improving prediction accuracy and reduces design uncertainty, thereby enhancing infrastructure resilience and public safety. Also, digital twins offer the potential of real-time simulation and optimization for geotechnical systems. Challenges like data quality, sensor durability, interoperability, reliability of acquired data and its interpretation are present in the current scenario, necessitating interdisciplinary collaboration and development of standard protocols for deployment in the field in case of full-fledged adaptation. AI and IoT can redefine geotechnical engineering practice and open pathways for sustainable infrastructure that is resilient and adaptive. This review aims to summarize the development and available techniques that have been explored and reported in geotechnical engineering using AI and IoT, highlighting the need for progress in this direction. © 2027 selection and editorial matter, Vedprakash C. Source title: 2026 International Conference on Sustainable and Futuristic Technologies, ICSFT 2026
Affiliations: Prmceam Badnera-Amravati, Department of Electrical Engineering, Maharashtra, India; Government College of Engineering Amravati, Department of Electrical Engineering, Maharashtra, India
Authors with affiliations: Dahane A.S., Prmceam Badnera-Amravati, Department of Electrical Engineering, Maharashtra, India; Sharma R.B., Government College of Engineering Amravati, Department of Electrical Engineering, Maharashtra, India
Abstract: In fast converter switching, volatile renewable injections, frequent mode changes, and partial observability, hybrid AC-DC microgrids must behave like a power systems. This tension requires validation frameworks beyond nominal models and idealized control assumptions. Most research used fixedparameter simulations, poorly coupled digital twins, or controller tuning evaluated under limited disturbance sets, which seems to leave a gap between stated performance and field behavior, especially at AC-DC interfaces. A, chained validation and control treats model mismatch, uncertainty and explainability as a key signals, but not subsidiary issues. In this paper a five-step analytical procedure is established. Here, hybrid Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) Twin-Fidelity Calibrator calibrates parameters and structures residual fingerprints by aligning averaged and electromagnetic transient models. This residual goes directly into a Residual-Aware Distributionally Constrained Hybrid MPC (Model Predictive Control), where Wasserstein ambiguity impacts control decisions under observed deviations rather than presumed noise. Causal Graph Neural State and Fault Trajectories and constraint-activity traces are processed by the attribution layer to isolate strong instability drivers while maintaining physical directionality across AC and DC subsystems. Based on this belief state, a Barrier-Certified Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning coordinator adjusts converter operations during fast transients while respecting safety invariants in the process. To generate safety margins instead of qualitative statements, a Hybrid Contract Verification and Counterfactual Stress Prover evaluates learned rules against targeted adversarial scenarios. Experimental validation on representative hybrid microgrid shows lower voltage and frequency excursions, faster post islanding recovery, and quantified safe operating envelope extensions. Evidence-driven, falsification-aware microgrid control designs may replace performance-centric validation. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Future Trends and Innovations

Authors with affiliations: Bai S., Department of Civil and Engineering, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Li X., Department of Civil and Engineering, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Zhu W., Department of Civil and Engineering, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong
Abstract: This chapter reviews the evolving technology landscape of industrialized construction (IC) through the integration of automation, robotics, and artificial intelligence (AI). Rather than treating innovations as isolated tools, it adopts a functional, closed-loop view-linking sensing and localization, execution semantics and modeling, decision and optimization, execution and control, and verification and compliance-to explain how task chains can produce computable states, constraint-aware decisions, and auditable outcomes across the factory-logistics-site continuum. It further examines the shift of AI from recognition-oriented applications toward executable decision support, including the emerging roles of generative AI and digital twins as runtime systems for prediction and rolling replanning under uncertainty. Next-generation robotics is synthesized as process-embedded execution units for material handling and assembly, connection and closure, surface finishing, and autonomous construction equipment, alongside construction-scale additive manufacturing. Despite the technological strides, the chapter addresses the challenges these innovations face, including the unpredictable nature of construction sites and the slow integration of AI into established workflows. Looking forward, the text discusses the potential for a transformative impact on IC through the synergy of AI, robotics, and modular construction techniques, which could lead to more sustainable. © 2026 Xiao Li.

Title: ADAPTING PROJECTION-BASED REDUCED-ORDER MODELS USING PROJECTED GAUSSIAN PROCESS

Abstract: Projection-based model reduction is among the most widely adopted methods for constructing parametric reduced-order models (ROMs). Utilizing the snapshot data from solving full-order governing equations, the proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) computes the optimal basis modes that represent the data, and a ROM can be constructed in the low-dimensional vector subspace spanned by the POD basis. For parametric governing equations, a potential challenge arises when there is a need to update the POD basis to adapt ROMs that accurately capture the variation of a system's behavior over its parameter space (in design, control, uncertainty quantification, digital twins applications, etc.). In this paper, we propose a projected Gaussian process (pGP) and formulate the problem of adapting the POD basis as a supervised statistical learning problem, for which the goal is to learn a mapping from the parameter space to the Grassmann manifold that contains the optimal subspaces. A mapping is first established between the Euclidean space and the horizontal space of an orthogonal matrix that spans a reference subspace in the Grassmann manifold. A second mapping from the horizontal space to the Grassmann manifold is established through the exponential/logarithm maps between the manifold and its tangent space. Finally, given a new parameter, the conditional distribution of a vector can be found in the Euclidean space using the Gaussian process (GP) regression, and such a distribution is then projected to the Grassmann manifold that enables us to predict the optimal subspace for the new parameter. As a statistical learning approach, the proposed pGP allows us to optimally estimate (or tune) the model parameters from data and quantify the statistical uncertainty associated with the prediction. The advantages of the proposed pGP are demonstrated by numerical experiments. © 2026 Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics

Abstract: The complexity of today's modern waste management systems is rising due to the sustainable development of the circular economy and sustainability mandates, demanding decision framework integrating beyond conventional cost–benefit approach. Based on this, a hybrid model that combines the thermodynamic performance analysis, the lifecycle assessment, and the fuzzy multicriteria decision-making is proposed to suggest the recovery pathways in circular waste systems. The model provides the economic and environmental evaluation model incorporating fuzzy logic to address the uncertainties in economic and environmental evaluations in system boundaries, stakeholder preferences, and data variations. An architecture that integrates the energy efficiency metrics with the socioeconomic and lifecycle impact criteria is developed as a multilayering architecture. The framework is demonstrated to provide better accuracy and insight for decision-making on waste recovery policy alternatives and on siting and operating waste landfills or recovery facilities. Finally, the chapter summarizes barriers referring to implementation, policy implications, and prospects for future research about artificial intelligence– enhanced fuzzy systems and digital twins in relation to sustainable waste management. © 2026 Scrivener Publishing LLC.

Affiliations: Quantum Serbia, Serbia; Serbian AI Association, Serbia

Abstract: How do data become social capital – more than a corporate asset, a measurable public good that improves health, equity, and sustainability? This chapter answers across four arcs. First, it tracks the analytic stack from OLAP and data mining to Big Data, Deep Learning (DL), and causal, privacy-preserving pipelines, marking the shift from hindsight to intervention. Second, it frames Society 5.0 as human-centred by design: explainability, fairness, and documented governance as operating requirements within edge–core architectures which keep people in the loop. Third, it examines substrates which make real-time analytics feasible at acceptable cost: neuromorphic spiking networks at the edge, photonic linear layers for matrix-heavy inference, and quantum-assisted routines where structure and noise budgets permit – judged by energy per decision, latency, and audit trails rather than headline FLOPS. Finally, applications ground the argument: clinical CNNs, legal Natural Language Processing (NLP), federated learning (FL) for data sovereignty, SHAP for recourse, and physics-informed digital twins which enable therapy planning before intervention. Organoid intelligence (OI) is treated with scientific caution – as exploratory, protocol-sensitive co-processing. The result is a pragmatic roadmap: align models with social outcomes, measure uncertainty and energy, document decisions, and preserve agency – so analytics functions as a civic capability in Society 5.0. © 2027 selection and editorial matter, Amarnath Padhi, Sabyasachi Rath, Elena Gurgu, and Dac-Nhuong Le; individual chapters, the contributors.

Title: Toward AI-assisted digital force metrology: A vision for the digital metrology avatar

Authors with affiliations: Vikas, CSIR National Physical Laboratory, New Delhi, India; Tewari K., Force and Hardness Metrology Group, New Delhi, India; Gautam S.K., Force and Hardness Metrology Group, New Delhi, India; Kumar K., Force and Hardness Metrology Group, New Delhi, India; Kumar R., Force and Hardness Metrology Group, New Delhi, India
Abstract: Force metrology is undergoing a paradigm shift from conventional hardware-centric sensing toward smart measurement systems enabled by the confluence of novel sensors, computational imaging, optical metrology, and artificial intelligence (AI). The article presents a forward-looking perspective on how these emerging technologies may collectively reshape the future of force metrology. Rather than a complete measurement system, the article describes the concept of a Digital Metrology Avatar as a self-powered, computationally extensible, intelligent, and traceable representation of a physical force measurement system that can perform traceable sensing, computational imaging, intelligent inference, and digital metrology services in a connected measurement ecosystem. To illustrate the feasibility of this vision, we present a representative proof-of-concept case based on a precision flexure transducer and laser speckle pattern imaging. The example demonstrates how experimentally observable elastic deformation features can be extracted using Fourier optics and phase correlation image processing and subsequently correlated with the applied force using Gaussian process regression. By building upon the example and the recent developments in non-contact sensing, the article gives a vision of how software-based, AI-assisted metrology could be realized in force metrology by utilizing uncertainty-aware AI, digital twins, digitalized calibration infrastructures, and explainable AI methods. © 1998-2012 IEEE.
